articles.title: Sussex horse lover's final wish fulfilled with hospice pony visit
articles.summary: Denise Lee was able to spend time with two ponies at a hospice after her daughter appealed for help.
articles.body:
A lifelong horse lover was able to spend time with two ponies in the final days of her life after a community appeal helped arrange a surprise hospice visit.

Denise Lee, from Ashington, West Sussex, had loved horses since childhood and volunteered with the Riding for the Disabled Association but her cancer diagnosis meant she could no longer ride.

While receiving care at St Barnabas House in Worthing last month, she told the hospice's staff she would love to touch a horse and experience the "horsey smell" again.

A healthcare assistant suggested trying to make the wish happen and Joanne, Denise's daughter, appealed for help through local Facebook community groups.

"She was a horse lover from I think the age of like five or six," Joanne said.

"She loved all animals, but horses were really special to her. So she rode throughout her whole life."

The post was spotted by Kerry Saunders, from Ashington, who offered to bring two Shetland ponies to the hospice.

Staff helped move Denise's bed into a courtyard so she could meet the animals and stroke them, with family members, including her granddaughters, Sassi, aged eight, and Phoebe, aged seven, also there.

"The horses walked round the corner and there wasn't a dry eye in the place," Joanne said.

"Everyone was crying. The staff were there. Her grandchildren were there. We were all there. And it was the most special memory."

Joanne described the response to her appeal as "overwhelming".

The visit took place on Friday 14 August, the last day that her mother was fully conscious, she said, adding: "It was the last wonderful day that we got to spend with her doing something that we know that she loved and wanted to do."

Kerry Saunders said Denise's face "just lit up".

"She was able to stroke them and feel their breath, which is exactly what she wanted," she said.

The former nurse added: "I just felt so privileged to be able to fulfil one of her last wishes, and the ponies were absolutely amazing.

She said the ponies also visited another patient after staff were asked if they could stop by a second room.

Joanne said it was a "fantastic" day that she would look back on with happy memories.

She said: "There's that spark of joy in otherwise what was such an emotionally difficult weekend."

articles.title: Teen's lost Coventry archive found after six decades in attic
articles.summary: Photographer Elizabeth Tyler rediscovered the images, now donated to City Archives, in her attic.
articles.body:
In 1963, 17-year-old Elizabeth Tyler wandered the streets of Coventry capturing images of the city's bomb sites and abandoned buildings.

The teenager, from Leamington Spa, had just lost both of her parents suddenly leaving her homeless, and said photography offered an escape from her own circumstances.

Now, aged 80 and living in southern Sweden, Tyler rediscovered the box of pictures, which has resulted in her first-ever photography exhibition and book.

"[Photography] helped me forget about my own situation," she said.

"I could just concentrate on what I saw through the lens."

She found accommodation at the city's YWCA, which was "cold and damp, everything smelt of mould, but it was the only home I had then," she explained.

With her first wages from an evening job as a waitress, she bought a 1933 Rolleicord camera and enrolled as a student at the Coventry College of Art.

Mornings were spent looking for interesting subjects to photograph, and she would develop the films each afternoon in the college's darkroom.

"I didn't really know much about aperture, film speed or shutter speed," she said.

"But that didn't bother me, I found inspiration in everything I looked at."

Much of her photography focussed on the Hillfields area of the city, where, 20 years after the blitz, there was still devastation.

"The people who still lived there fascinated me," she explained. "It was a real eye-opener for me."

Some of the images show children playing among rubble-strewn streets.

Others capture empty rooms in abandoned buildings that the student explored as a curious teenager.

"I was quite brave," she recalled, "I went into some of these buildings just to see what they looked like."

After completing her studies in 1965, she left Coventry for an au pair job in Stockholm, taking the box of images with her.

Unable to afford the cost of developing the negatives after leaving college, she turned to drawing and painting.

"I could afford a block of paper and a pen, so I did these ink drawings instead," she explained, a change that would help shape her life.

In 1966, Tyler had her first art exhibition in Istanbul, before becoming a successful artist with her work shown in many cities across the world.

The images from Coventry survived being moved to four different countries, over six decades, and remained untouched in a box in her attic, she explained.

"One day about six months ago, I thought maybe they're up there and it could be fun to see what they look like now," she explained.

After eventually discovering the box and digitising the images, she explained how she had started sharing them on a Coventry local history Facebook group.

"I just put up one photograph, and a lot of people commented, and so I put up another and then one photograph per day for two months."

The images are on display in an exhibition until 8 October as part of Coventry Then & Now at LTB Showrooms in the city.

The exhibition proved so popular it was extended, the venue said.

"I think it's great," the photographer added. "I would have loved to have been there."

She has also donated digital copies of the images to City Archives at the Herbert Art Gallery & Museum.

In addition, the public can view the prints in the museum's research room.

The images have also been published in a book , Elizabeth Tyler — Coventry 1960s, by Cafe Royal Books.

The original Rolleicord no longer works, she explained, but had been gifted to her eldest son who became a photographer.

The box of images had survived 20 years in Denmark, eight in Finland and 30 years in her Swedish attic.

"My whole family are all very proud of me," the grandmother of three added.

articles.title: Prefeita de Divinópolis é internada no CTI após passar mal em casa | G1
articles.standfirst: Janete foi encaminhada a um hospital, onde passou por avaliação e exames. Segundo a Prefeitura, quadro de saúde é estável.
articles.summary: A prefeita de Divinópolis, Janete Aparecida, apresenta quadro estável no CTI após passar mal e suspender compromissos oficiais para realizar exames hospitalares neste sábado.
articles.body:
Janete Aparecida passou mal no sá — Foto: Câmara de Divinópolis/Divulgação

A prefeita de Divinópolis Janete Aparecida, de 51 anos, passou mal em casa na tarde de sábado (3) e precisou ser encaminhada para um hospital. Segundo a Prefeitura, ela foi avaliada por médicos e permanece internada no Centro de Tratamento Intensivo (CTI) neste domingo (4) por precaução. O quadro de saúde da prefeita é estável.

Conforme a Prefeitura, o Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) foi acionado para atender a prefeita. Como, naquele momento, todas as equipes estavam empenhadas em outros atendimentos, a orientação médica foi para que ela procurasse atendimento hospitalar por meios próprios.

Na sequência, Janete foi levada ao hospital, onde passou por avaliação e realizou exames.

Por causa da internação, os compromissos oficiais de Janete Aparecida estão temporariamente suspensos.

Em nota, a Prefeitura agradeceu as manifestações de carinho e informou que novas informações sobre o estado de saúde da prefeita serão divulgadas oportunamente.

Dr Furlan (PSD), candidato ao governo do Amapá, vota em Macapá. — Foto: Francisco Pinheiro/g1

O candidato ao governo do Amapá Dr Furlan ( PSD ) votou neste domingo (4), pela manhã, na Escola Estadual Profª. Raimunda Virgolino, no bairro Pedrinhas, em Macapá . Ele chegou ao local de votação por volta de 9h30 acompanhado da esposa e candidata ao Senado, Rayssa Furlan ( Podemos ), filhos e membros do partido.

Após votar, Dr. Furlan falou sobre a possibilidade de vitória no primeiro turno e sobre o trabalho realizado durante sua gestão como prefeito da capital.

“A expectativa é de vitória no primeiro turno. Todas as pesquisas há mais de um ano mostram que nós temos números consolidados e que nós vamos vencer a eleição no primeiro turno, fazendo a vontade do povo do Amapá . Durante cinco anos e dois meses nós mostramos à frente da Prefeitura de Macapá que é possível trabalhar, realizar, entregar obras a todo instante, é possível estar ao lado do povo, é possível mudar a vida da população para melhor. E hoje a gente chega aqui com as bênçãos de Deus, com a vontade do povo do Amapá e nós vamos vencer a eleição para o governo do Estado, vamos também fazer os dois senadores, uma bancada forte para que a gente consiga trabalhar e fazer as entregas que o povo tanto espera do próximo governador”, disse.

articles.title: Rafael Fonteles (PT) vota em Teresina | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato ao governo do Piauí votou neste domingo (4) no Colégio Madre Savina, na Zona Leste da capital.
articles.summary: Candidato ao governo do Piauí votou neste domingo (4) no Colégio Madre Savina, na Zona Leste da capital.
articles.body:
Rafael Fonteles (PT) vota em Teresina — Foto: Aric Lages/g1

O candidato à reeleição, governador Rafael Fonteles (PT), votou neste domingo (4), no Colégio Madre Savina, na Zona Leste de Teresina . Ele chegou ao local de votação por volta de 9h40, acompanhado da família e apoiadores.

Rafael Fonteles disse estar confiante no resultado das urnas e destacou a mobilização de apoiadores durante a campanha.

"Aproveitar o momento para agradecer toda essa caminhada, todos que nos ajudaram, nos apoiaram. Nesse momento vamos aguardar de forma muito serena a decisão do povo do Piauí e do Brasil. Estou muito confiante, muito otimista, mas com muita humildade, aguardando aí a vontade soberana do povo, que vai escolher os seus representantes, não apenas o governador, presidente, mas também os parlamentares que vão atuar no processo de eleição para decidir os destinos do Brasil e do Piauí. Eu, particularmente, coloquei minhas propostas de maneira muito clara para que a população possa decidir. É uma candidatura à reeleição, então tudo o que nós fizemos, além dos caminhos que nós estamos apontando para o futuro, será um objeto de avaliação por parte da população. E o nível do Brasil continua muito polarizado, muito acirrado, mas eu estou muito confiante na vitória do presidente Lula também", comentou.

Os 2,7 milhões de eleitores aptos a votar no Piauí vão às urnas neste domingo (4), no primeiro turno das eleições de 2026. Eles poderão escolher entre 323 candidaturas aprovadas pela Justiça Eleitoral para os cargos de deputado estadual, deputado federal, senador, governador e presidente da República.

Caso seja necessário, o segundo turno para presidente e governador será realizado em 25 de outubro. O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Piauí (TRE-PI) prevê divulgar o resultado oficial da apuração dos votos no estado até as 21h.

Para garantir a segurança da eleição, a Polícia Militar do Piauí mobilizou cerca de 6.500 policiais. Desse total, aproximadamente 3.500 atuarão diretamente nos locais de votação. Os demais serão responsáveis pelo policiamento ostensivo em diferentes regiões e zonas eleitorais.

A Polícia Civil do Piauí também reforçará a operação e designou 320 profissionais para auxiliar a Polícia Judiciária da União. O efetivo é composto por 70 delegados e 250 oficiais investigadores.

Além disso, cerca de 2.800 militares do Exército Brasileiro vão reforçar a segurança em 143 municípios piauienses durante o primeiro turno. O contingente inclui militares que já atuam no estado e reforços enviados por Pernambuco e Bahia.

Passageiros e funcionários do Aeroporto de Teresina poderão votar ou justificar a ausência nas eleições diretamente no terminal durante o primeiro turno. Segundo a administração do aeroporto, a estrutura foi montada pelo Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Piauí (TRE-PI) e funcionará na área administrativa.

articles.title: William Siri vota em Campo Grande, na Zona Oeste do Rio | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do Psol ao Governo do Rio de Janeiro estava acompanhado da mulher e da filha. Ele afirma que irá para o segundo turno.
articles.summary: William Siri (Psol), candidato ao Governo do Rio de Janeiro, chegou para votar neste domingo (4). Ele votou na Escola Municipal Professora Marita de Vasconcelos, em Campo Grande.
articles.body:
William Siri votou em Campo Grande, na Zona Oeste do Rio — Foto: Mateus Castro/ TV Globo

O candidato ao governo do Rio de Janeiro William Siri ( Psol ) chegou para votar neste domingo (4). Ele esteve na Escola Municipal Professora Marita de Vasconcelos, em Campo Grande, na Zona Oeste do Rio de Janeiro, às 9h57.

Siri estava acompanhado da mulher e da filha. Antes de votar, cumprimentou eleitores. O candidato do Psol elogiou a mobilização dos brasileiros para a votação.

“Primeiro, hoje é uma festa da democracia muito importante. O povo está indo às urnas para votar no que realmente confia”, afirmou.

Siri estava acompanhado da mulher e da filha — Foto: Mateus Castro/ TV Globo

Siri afirmou que acredita em uma votação “incrível” e que irá para o segundo turno da eleição para governador do Rio de Janeiro. Ele acompanhará parte da apuração com a família e depois se encontrará com a militância do Psol.

“A gente vai para o segundo turno, eu estou muito animado porque as ruas estão demonstrando isso. Depois do debate da TV Globo, principalmente, sentimos que o jogo virou para o segundo turno. Eu vou continuar com a minha família, com a minha filhinha, com a minha esposa. Vou ficar com elas até o final da tarde”, disse Siri.

William Siri, candidato do PSOL ao governo do Rio, foi entrevistado pelo RJ1 — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Aos 33 anos, William Carlos Brum Bispo, o William Siri, disputa o cargo de governador pela primeira vez. Ele é economista e vereador do Rio de Janeiro.

Nascido em Nova Iguaçu, na Baixada Fluminense, ele se mudou para Campo Grande com 10 anos. Eleito para a Câmara Municipal da capital fluminense em 2020 e reeleito em 2024, com 19.800 votos.

O candidato ao governo de Mato Grosso do Sul, Delcídio Amaral ( PRD ) votou neste domingo (4) em uma escola particular em Corumbá . Ele chegou ao local de votação por volta de 9h34. articles.title: Dale Martin: Derby father of murder victim says trial was 'hell'
articles.summary: Dale Martin says some of his son's killers would come to his house for evening meals as children.
articles.body:
The father of a man who was fatally attacked by an armed gang has described the trial following his son's death as "hell".

Dale Martin, also known as DJ, was dragged out of a car in Derby in June 2025 and repeatedly stabbed and slashed.

On Friday, one man was was given a life sentence , with a minimum term of 27 years, for his murder. Five other men from the city - who were found guilty of manslaughter following a trial more than four months long - were also jailed.

Speaking to the BBC after the sentencing hearing, the victim's father, Dale Martin, said some of the killers went to the same school as his son, and some would come to his house for evening meals as children.

"Some of these children used to hang about on the street late at night, and if we were about and we were cooking tea, someone would come in and have tea in the garden or in the kitchen with us," Martin added.

Martin, said he felt "relief" that court proceedings had now concluded.

"It's been nearly five months of hell to be fair, something we've never gone through and I'd never want to go through it again," he said.

"It hurts, we're just going to go home as a family and just try and get back to some sort of normality which it never will do.

"It'll never come to normality because DJ's not there," Martin added.

"He's always in our thoughts, always in our hearts, he's always here with me, it's just hard and I'm just glad it's all over."

The attack - the court in Loughborough heard - followed a history of "animosity" between two rival groups, stretching back years, and two "tit for tat" confrontations earlier that weekend.

Martin was attacked near to where he had been attending a gender-reveal party several hours earlier at a pub.

The court heard a Renault Megane he was travelling in was ambushed when, "in a show of force", the group put their electric bikes in the road to stop the car, which then swerved and stalled.

Adrian Langdale KC, prosecuting, told the trial, attackers had armed themselves with swords, machetes and "Rambo knives".

Martin was pulled from the car through a smashed window and initially managed to escape, but then tripped on a piece of wood.

His attackers set upon him "like a pack of animals", a witness had told the court.

"Nobody deserves to die the way he died over a 'tit for tat'," Martin said.

"It's just horrible, it's horrible, but he was a lovely lad and he'll be forever missed by a lot of people."

Paying tribute to his son, Martin said the memory he would miss the most was his "smile".

"He was just a proper family lad with a heart of gold and he'd do anything for his family."

Judge Gregory Dickinson KC handed Jayden Mannion-Roberts, 26, of Tennyson Street in Derby, a life sentence, with a minimum term of 27 years, for Martin's murder.

Ki Grant-Finlayson, 23, of Addison Road was sentenced to an 18-year jail term, with a three-year extended licence on release for his "leading role" in the ambush.

Keenan Hamblett, 27, of Osmaston Park Road, was sentenced to 17 and a half years, and Shaylon McCalla, 27, of Copes Way, received 18 years, with a three-year extended licence.

Grant-Finlayson and Hamblett tried to fly one-way to Tunisia following the attack but were arrested at Gatwick airport, each with about £3,000 in cash, the court heard.

The judge gave "enthusiastic participants" in the attack, Kayin Holmes, 25, of Nightingale Road, 15 years, and Kelci Thompson, 19, of Osmaston Road, 10 years, to be served in a young offenders institution.

Dale's younger sister said the 21-year-old was a "very big part" of her life and said "towards the end is when we got closer, we went everywhere together".

"I spent most of my time with him, and it's just hard not having him here," she said.

articles.title: Bosnia votes in one of world’s most complicated general elections
articles.summary: Voters cast their ballots for a dizzying number of officials across multiple tiers of government.
articles.body:
Polls have opened in Bosnia and Herzegovina for a general election to choose new leaders at the national and regional levels, in a vote that could affect the country’s European Union membership bid.

On Saturday, about 3.4 million voters are choosing the three members of the country’s multiethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national Parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs.

Bosnia’s complex web of governing institutions was created by a United States-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the 1992-95 war.

The major parties’ repeated focus on war-era rhetoric and division was frustrating for some voters, activist Adi Selman of the Karton Revolucija protest group told the AFP news agency.

“I don’t think these new elections in Bosnia will change anything,” the 34-year-old said in the northern Bosnian town of Tuzla, ahead of the vote.

“The choice is limited to political parties that have already been around for 30 years and basically pick up votes by harping on about war, tensions, divisions and the past.”

“Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead; it is an impossible country,” Republika Srpska’s former president, Milorad Dodik, told the final rally of his right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) in the entity’s capital Banja Luka late on Friday.

In the FBiH, Bosniak parties are pushing for a stronger central state, with incumbent Bosniak presidency member Denis Becirovic pledging a renewed path to the EU and NATO.

The EU granted Bosnia candidate status in December 2022, but accession negotiations scheduled for 2024 were delayed as Brussels demanded the country pass stronger anticorruption laws and reform its judicial system.

Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform, demanding a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.

Meanwhile, Russia is accused of slowing down the country’s path towards joining the EU, while also holding close ties with the SNSD, which favours secession for Republika Srpska.

This general election is the first in the country in which new electronic tools are being used to scan ballot papers and carry out biometric fingerprint verification in a move to reduce fraud during the election.

Polls close at 7pm (17:00 GMT) and first results are expected later on Sunday.

articles.title: Photos: Community unites in Senegal’s Dakar to clean dilapidated school
articles.summary: Volunteers and students prepare safer, cleaner classrooms in advance of the academic year in Senegal’s capital.
articles.body:
Students, teachers and volunteers in a working-class Dakar neighbourhood have joined forces to clean up the dilapidated Medina Gounass Elementary School in advance of the new academic year, highlighting wider concerns over public education and sanitation in Senegal’s capital.

On Saturday, pupils, members of environmental organisations and residents swept classrooms, cleared drains and collected piles of plastic and household waste from the school in Medina Gounass, a densely populated suburb of Dakar.

The initiative comes as the 2026-27 school year is set to begin on Monday for staff and Tuesday for students.

Footage from the scene shows young students wielding brooms and shovels alongside older volunteers.

Medina Gounass, like many outlying districts of Dakar, struggles with inadequate waste management, blocked drainage and overcrowded classrooms, problems that often worsen during the rainy season.

Organisers say the cleanup is meant not only to ready the school for reopening but also to raise awareness among students and residents about the importance of environmental protection and shared responsibility for public spaces.

articles.title: In 2013, a New Jersey teacher saw workers mowing a solar field near home and asked to bring in her sheep; by 2021, her flock had grown from 50 sheep on 15 solar acres to 450 sheep managing 85 acres
articles.summary: What began with a simple observation beside a solar field turned into an unusual farming business in New Jersey.
articles.body: What began with a simple observation beside a solar field turned into an unusual farming business in New Jersey. When Julie Bishop noticed workers repeatedly mowing vegetation beneath and around solar panels, she saw an opportunity to put her sheep to work instead. What started as a small flock grazing a single site eventually grew into a full-time solar-grazing operation, pairing livestock with renewable-energy infrastructure, states an online observation piece by the Cornell University’s College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.From six acres to solar fieldsAccording to the website report, Bishop's journey into solar grazing began at her six-acre farm in Newfield, New Jersey. With limited pasture available and a growing need for space for her sheep, she began looking for alternative grazing land.A fenced solar array caught her attention. Instead of relying on machinery to keep vegetation under control, the site could be managed naturally by grazing animals. Bishop approached the solar company and eventually secured a vegetation-management contract. Solar Sheep LLC was born from that arrangement. The operation initially involved around 50 sheep grazing 15 acres of solar panels. By 2021, Bishop was managing approximately 85 acres across multiple solar sites with a flock of 450 sheep.Sheep as solar-site workersAs per the report, solar grazing requires considerably more planning than simply turning livestock loose in a field. Bishop uses portable fencing where a site allows it, creating paddocks that can be rotated as the flock moves through the vegetation. Not every solar installation is suited to extensive fencing, however. At smaller or awkwardly shaped sites, she relies on water and mineral stations to encourage the sheep to move toward areas that need attention. Transport is another part of the operation. Bishop uses a 24-foot stock trailer capable of carrying about 50 sheep at a time, while her Australian Cattle Dog, Mandy, helps gather the flock and locate animals during moves between sites.The flock consists primarily of mature yearlings and ewes. Lambs remain at the home farm, where Bishop can closely monitor their health and development. She raises Katahdin sheep, with lambing generally taking place in January and February. The resulting lambs are sold for meat, pets and to other solar grazers.A business that keeps expandingThe growing operation has also taken Bishop beyond routine vegetation management. Her experience has led to involvement in the planning of a proposed 700-acre utility-scale solar facility designed specifically for grazing. The planned site includes infrastructure such as lambing barns, feed storage, water and electricity, allowing sheep to remain on the property throughout the year. Bishop's expanding flock was expected to approach 1,000 animals as the operation developed.Solar grazing still comes with practical complications. Trucks and trailers must navigate sites that were often designed for equipment rather than livestock, while gates, cable trays and electrical infrastructure require careful coordination.Building a wider solar-grazing communityIt also states that Bishop became a member of the American Solar Grazing Association, finding value in a network focused on sharing knowledge and improving the way livestock and solar installations can coexist. Her experience also brought her a position as an ASGA board advisor, taking her work beyond her own flock. What started as a vision of sheep-shaped potential in a field of solar panels has emerged as a model for how farming and renewable-energy infrastructure can co-exist on the same land.Image Courtesy: Cornell University’s College of Agriculture and Life SciencesYou use AI every day. articles.title: The story of a book in Gaza: A treasured possession given new lease of life
articles.summary: With libraries, schools and homes destroyed in Gaza, surviving books have become treasured possessions.
articles.body:
Aya al-Shawa, 10, sits in sixth grade at a school in northern Gaza, holding a book she recently received and what is now one of her most treasured possessions.

Before it reached Aya’s hands, it had a difficult journey. It once sat on a bookshelf before an Israeli attack demolished the building it was housed in, leaving it buried beneath the rubble. Then one day someone recovered it, cleaned it, sorted its pages and repaired them. The book then found its way to a new reader.

Amid the widespread destruction in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, books – one of the most vulnerable of all items – have become a rare commodity.

About 98 percent of school buildings in the Gaza Strip have been destroyed or damaged, according to UNICEF.

With approximately 700,000 children in Gaza deprived of regular in-person education since the war began in October 2023, books have also become a vital way for children to reconnect with learning.

UNESCO has documented widespread damage to cultural sites and institutions in Gaza, including libraries. With a “ceasefire” in Gaza since October 2025, during which there has been a relative decrease in Israeli bombing, books have begun to take a second life.

Mohammed Saad, 54, from Beit Lahiya, has spent more than 35 years collecting books, and before the war, he estimated that he had between 50,000 and 100,000 titles in his library.

On December 7, 2023, the library was destroyed.

After being displaced 16 times in total, Saad returned to Beit Lahiya again to see what remained of his book collection. From the rubble of his home, he began to pull out the surviving books.

“I risked my life to save these books from beneath the rubble,” Saad said.

He managed to recover about 12,000 books from the rubble and moved what he could to Deir el-Balah, where he erected a tent and established a library called Athar, meaning “impact” but also relating to antiquities or historical relics.

From the tent, Saad and his son Mohammed began cleaning and repairing the thousands of books in their possession.

But Saad’s goal is not only to save the books from damage. He also wants them to reach people, particularly children.

The library now sees children coming every day, looking for stories that might help them find some escape from their hardships.

They buy some of them at symbolic prices ranging from 5 shekels to 15 shekels ($1.63-$4.89), given that books have become unaffordable for most families.

Giving children access to books is a key reason for saving them in the first place: to keep knowledge accessible and give them a path back to reading and learning despite war and displacement.

But the books Saad rescues still face other dangers. Inside the tent, there is little protection from the sun, heat, humidity and rain.

“I saved them from beneath the rubble and from the fire. Today, I cannot save them from the rain,” Saad said.

Elsewhere, Omar Hamad, 30, a displaced person from Beit Hanoon in northern Gaza, has also been searching for destroyed libraries for books.

He traced the locations of libraries in northern Gaza and Gaza City and contacted their owners. So far, Hamad says, he and his team have extricated some 3,000 books.

Not all of the books came from rubble. Some were donated by the families of people who were killed and had private libraries, while the team bought or reprinted others.

Among the books Omar rescued was The Catastrophe of Palestine, printed in 1956. He found it in the destroyed Islamic University of Gaza library , where books were scattered among the rubble.

Retrieving the book was only the beginning of his task.

Omar and his friend Ibrahim cleaned the books, removed dust and traces of rubble, sorted and arranged the pages, and tried to repair whatever they could.

When a book required more specialised restoration, he turned to Jameel Mikdad, 71, in the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.

Mikdad has worked in bookbinding and book repair for more than 45 years. His library and printing shop were destroyed during the war, but he continued working with limited resources, using his experience to rearrange pages, glue torn sections of the works, sew books and rebind them.

There is no single cost for repairing a book; it depends on the extent of the damage and the materials required. But the cost of materials has risen sharply.

Mikdad says a 3kg (6.6-pound) container of white glue cost 30-35 shekels ($9.78-11.48) before the war. Its price has now risen to 450-500 shekels ($146.74-163.05) due to Israel’s siege on Gaza and the damage caused by the war.

Repairing a damaged book can take two days to a week, depending on its condition. Sometimes the cost of repair can exceed the value of the book.

Not every book can be repaired. Omar says some of the books they found were 80 or 90 percent damaged and had to be left behind because they were no longer repairable or restorable.

At other times, they kept books that could no longer be read because bullet holes or fire damage made them witnesses to the genocide in Gaza.

“We took them with us so they could remain witnesses to this crime,” Omar said.

For the books that can be saved, Omar does not want them to remain on library shelves but to be distributed throughout a population known for their love of literature.

At the Phoenix Library, books are lent rather than sold. Readers can borrow one or two books a week after paying a refundable deposit of 50 shekels ($16.30). The library has books on literature, medicine, law, history, economics and science. There are also books for children and for students related to specialised fields of study.

Omar also organises initiatives to deliver books to students at schools, so they can be used once again for their original purpose: reading and learning.

Aya, 10, ends up with one such book: The Adventure of the Empty House by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.

She sees the novel as a way of continuing her education when schools, often taking the form of a crowded tent , struggle to resume their role in teaching children.

And so, the journey of the book is complete.

It began on a shelf in a home or library in Gaza before the building was levelled in one of Israel’s thousands of air raids. It then remained beneath the rubble for months before being rescued by a person who risked their life to rescue lost books. It was then passed on to a restoration expert who repaired and cleaned it. Finally, it ended up in the hands of a student who will continue to love learning and overcome Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

Ultimately, the book survived destruction and returned to its first purpose: to be opened and read.

articles.title: Iowa livestock farmer Dave Johnson hosts four wind turbines that bring in about $30,000 a year, calling the steady lease income the 401(k) he never had while he continues raising cattle and hogs
articles.summary: Iowa is known for its farms, but its landscape is also filled with wind turbines.
articles.body: Iowa is known for its farms, but its landscape is also filled with wind turbines. The state produced 59% of its energy from wind in 2023, the highest share of any US state. For many farmers, wind energy is not about politics or climate change. It is also a way to earn a steady income from their land.Dave Johnson, a livestock farmer in northern Iowa, leases part of his land to a utility that installed four wind turbines on his property, Vox reported. The turbines bring him about $30,000 a year in total. Johnson raises cattle and hogs and says he wanted his farm to generate more value.“I never had a 401(k),” Johnson said. “I farmed and stuck everything back into the farm. This is the 401(k) that I never had,” he told Vox.Johnson is a Republican and said he voted for Donald Trump. His son also has wind turbines on his farm. For Johnson, however, the turbines are mainly an economic decision. The steady income from them gives his farm another source of money at a time when farming can be difficult.Johnson is not the only farmer in the area who has chosen wind energy. Fred Koschmeder, a corn and soybean farmer near Johnson, also has turbines on his land. He too said he voted for Trump, but does not see wind energy as a political issue.“I don’t even look at it as a political thing,” Koschmeder said. “It is economic development. If you’ve got a chance to participate in something that brings value, I think you’re kind of foolish not to do it. It adds a lot of value to your farm and extra income, too.”Why wind became so important in IowaIowa has become a major wind-energy state for several reasons. The simplest one is that the state has strong winds. Iowa is not the windiest state in the Great Plains, but it is closer to large population centres such as Chicago, which need large amounts of electricity.The state also adopted policies supporting renewable energy early. Iowa became the first US state to establish a renewable portfolio standard in 1983. The policy required investor-owned utilities to contract for or own at least 105 megawatts of renewable energy.Iowa reached that target by 1999, according to Tom Wind, a crop farmer and electrical engineer who has worked in the wind sector for decades. Later, state and federal tax incentives helped wind energy expand further.Republican Senator Chuck Grassley also played a role in the growth of the industry. In the 1990s, he helped establish a federal tax credit for building wind farms. This eventually earned him the title of the “father” of Iowa wind energy.Farmers became an important part of the growth because turbines gave them another source of income. Crop prices and yields can change, while a wind turbine can provide relatively stable revenue of thousands of dollars each year.Farmers see wind as extra incomeFarming in Iowa has become more difficult in recent years. The price of some crops, including soybeans, has fallen, while farm expenses such as tractor repairs have increased with inflation.For farmers such as Johnson, wind energy provides an additional source of income alongside agriculture. He said the money from turbines can help farmers continue working on their land. Wind energy “is allowing farmers to stay on the farm,” Johnson said. “That helps rural America.”The financial benefit also extends beyond farmers. Steve Guyer, senior energy policy counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, said people across the state can benefit from wind power through energy costs.Iowa has relatively stable energy bills that are generally below the national average. According to financial firm Lazard, onshore wind was the cheapest source of energy in 2024, with or without tax credits.“All customers benefit from it,” Guyer said. “Although other costs may rise over time, the cost of the wind actually remains stable or lowers. When we factor that into the overall utility bill, it at least stabilizes the bill.”The wind industry also employs about 4,000 people in Iowa and attracts billions of dollars in capital investment. Mak Heddens, who runs the clean-energy coalition Power Up Iowa, said wind is the No. 1 taxpayer in a third of Iowa counties.Wind energy and politicsThe strong economic benefits of wind energy have helped it remain popular in a state that has become strongly Republican. Iowa voted for Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024, with Trump winning 94 of the state's 99 counties in 2024.That creates a contrast with Trump's long-standing opposition to wind energy. Trump has criticised wind power for years and has taken steps intended to slow the industry's growth.On Inauguration Day, Trump said, “We’re not going to do the wind thing,” while describing wind turbines as “Big, ugly wind mills” that “ruin your neighborhood.”Some Iowa Republicans who benefit from wind energy, however, are not particularly worried about Trump's position. Johnson said he does not pay much attention to Trump's comments about wind power. “I know he just shoots his mouth off,” Johnson said.When asked about an executive order pausing new approvals for wind projects, Johnson said he was not worried because wind energy has support among Republicans.Brent Siegrist, a Republican state representative, also said he was not concerned about Trump's statements. “I’ve got enough things to do in Iowa to worry about Washington, DC,” he said.Concerns over future projectsDespite the industry's economic strength, wind developers face uncertainty over federal policies. In January, last year, Trump signed an executive order directing agencies to pause new and renewed federal approvals and leases for onshore and offshore wind projects.Potential tariffs are another concern. Tariffs on countries such as China could increase the cost of wind turbines because some turbines contain foreign-made parts, even when the turbines themselves are manufactured in Iowa.“There is a certain level of nervousness in the market,” Manav Sharma, North America division CEO for Nordex Group, a wind turbine manufacturer with a production facility in Iowa, told KCRG.There are also concerns about federal tax incentives for clean energy. Some wind advocates and lawmakers worry that Congress could reduce incentives included in the Inflation Reduction Act.Ernie Goss, an economist at Creighton University, said, “I think the subsidies are the biggest issue. articles.title: Russia’s nuclear plants are ageing. Who will pay to dismantle them?
articles.summary: Moscow faces a huge decommissioning bill at home even as it expands its nuclear industry abroad.
articles.body:
The world often discusses the nuclear threat posed by Russia, but far less attention is paid to the nuclear risks within Russia itself, particularly those posed by ageing nuclear power plants, some of whose reactors are already more than 50 years old.

At the same time, Russia is building nuclear power plants around the world, from Turkiye to Bangladesh, while promoting nuclear energy as a “sustainable” alternative to fossil fuels. Russian President Vladimir Putin regularly meets with foreign leaders to discuss existing and potential nuclear projects. Yet one question remains largely overlooked: what happens to these nuclear facilities when they reach the end of their operational lives?

During the Soviet period, nuclear power plants were built across the USSR, including in Lithuania. As part of Lithuania’s accession to the European Union, the country was required to shut down the two Soviet-built reactors at the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant. The first reactor was closed in 2004 and the second in 2009. The decommissioning process has proved both extraordinarily expensive and time-consuming. By 2020, the estimated cost had reached 3.3 billion euros ($3.7bn), with only 49 percent of the planned work completed. The process, initially scheduled for completion in 2038, is now expected to continue until 2049.

Russia itself does not seem to be paying much attention to this question. Rosenergoatom plans to decommission 35 reactors. Yet the company’s own estimates point to a funding shortfall of approximately 18.7 billion euros, while the total estimated cost of decommissioning is about 21 billion euros. And these are Rosenergoatom’s own estimates. Actual decommissioning costs are usually significantly higher than initially projected. For example, the cost of decommissioning the former nuclear power plant in Lubmin, Germany, was initially estimated at 1 billion euros but is now estimated at 10 billion euros.

For the time being, however, Russia appears to be postponing the most costly stages of decommissioning. Rather than fully dismantling reactors soon after shutdown, it often places them in long-term “safe” storage, transferring much of the financial and technical burden into the future. Deferred dismantling does not solve the problem, but merely postpones the costly stages of decommissioning, which is particularly concerning given Russia’s existing funding gap.

Environmental NGO Bellona Foundation reports, based on Rosatom’s own projections, that by around 2037, Rosatom’s decommissioning and remediation obligations could exceed its net profit. Moreover, the longer decommissioning is delayed, the greater the associated financial, technical and safety risks are likely to become.

Another major issue is the legacy of radioactive waste. Russia has inherited approximately 774,000 cubic metres of radioactive waste from the Soviet Union. The upcoming decommissioning of 36 reactor units at eight nuclear power plants is expected to generate an additional 800,000 cubic metres of radioactive waste.

Russia already has experience of what happens when industries leave major environmental liabilities behind. In the Kemerovo region, where around half of Russia’s coal is produced, mountains of waste from coal mining scar the landscape. Some of this waste burns, polluting nearby communities. When coal companies go bankrupt, the cost of dealing with what they leave behind can fall to the state and local communities.

But nuclear waste and decommissioned reactors cannot simply be abandoned if the money runs out. The question therefore becomes even more important as Russia’s economic situation deteriorates: what will happen to all these megaprojects if the money needed to maintain, decommission and eventually dismantle them is no longer available?

The countries where Russia is building its numerous nuclear power plants should therefore think about what happens if these projects cannot be maintained or later decommissioned as planned. They need a Plan B in case something goes wrong in Russia. And, as history has repeatedly shown, Russia’s political situation can change unpredictably.

The political consequences of nuclear mismanagement can also be significant. The Chornobyl disaster demonstrated how the Soviet authorities’ attempts to suppress information and downplay the scale of the accident fuelled public distrust and disillusionment, contributing to growing social and political unrest in the late Soviet period. Today, Russia’s continued neglect of nuclear waste and repeated postponement of nuclear plant decommissioning could similarly create conditions for both another environmental catastrophe and growing social unrest, particularly if authorities once again respond to such a crisis with silence or attempts to conceal its scale.

These risks are compounded by Russia’s deteriorating economic situation. In an effort to sustain the war economy, the Russian government has also drastically weakened environmental regulations. National defence is now by far the largest single item in Russia’s federal budget, while environmental protection accounts for only a small fraction of government spending.

Environmental disasters have repeatedly demonstrated that the Russian regime is unwilling to prioritise long-term environmental safety. Russia continues to operate an ageing shadow fleet to transport oil, and the environmental risks associated with that fleet were highlighted by the 2024 Black Sea oil spill, when two ageing Russian tankers released thousands of tonnes of fuel oil into the sea. The spill was described as the Black Sea region’s worst environmental disaster in decades. This broader pattern of environmental negligence raises questions about how the country will manage its ageing nuclear infrastructure and the growing problem of nuclear waste.

These issues should therefore be raised at every international forum where Russia promotes its nuclear industry, such as COPs, where encountering Russian nuclear lobbyists is a common experience. Russia is seeking to secure its place in the future of energy while continuing to use energy as a tool for exerting political influence and power around the world.

All of these issues are particularly concerning because Russia continues to promote its nuclear industry internationally, while independent voices capable of scrutinising its environmental impacts and safety record are increasingly silenced in Russia. As documented in a recent report by the Environmental Crisis Group, repression and the departure of environmental experts and activists have severely weakened Russia’s environmental movement.

Bellona and Greenpeace have been declared “undesirable” organisations in Russia, while EcoDefence, which organised campaigns around environmental and nuclear issues, has been designated a “foreign agent”, and its members have faced criminal prosecution.

Environmental organisations outside Russia continue to draw attention to these risks. EcoDefence in exile, alongside other German activists, campaigns against continued European cooperation with the Russian nuclear industry, which has largely escaped the sanctions imposed on other parts of Russia’s energy sector. According to Vladimir Slivyak, co-chair of EcoDefence, this continued dependence on Russian nuclear technology and services could itself create vulnerabilities that Russia could potentially exploit for sabotage or political pressure.

The result is a shrinking capacity to independently monitor and expose environmental risks inside Russia. This creates a dangerous information gap: a nuclear accident could happen, its scale could be concealed or downplayed by the authorities, and the public could learn the full extent of the disaster only years or even decades later. This is what happened after the 1957 Mayak disaster, when the Soviet authorities concealed the accident and its consequences and did not publicly acknowledge the disaster until 1989, more than three decades later, while thousands of people were left to suffer the long-term consequences of radioactive contamination.

This lack of transparency makes Russia’s nuclear industry an international concern, not merely an energy issue. Its ageing infrastructure, weak environmental oversight and growing reliance on secrecy create risks that can extend well beyond Russia’s borders.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: 'Forced to say I wanted to work in sex racket': Newlywed alleges dowry torture, assault by husband
articles.summary: THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: A 24-year-old newlywed from Neendakara has alleged that her husband and his family subjected her to brutal physical and psychological
articles.body: THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: A 24-year-old newlywed from Neendakara has alleged that her husband and his family subjected her to brutal physical and psychological abuse over dowry, including kicking her in the abdomen, hitting her on the head with a pressure cooker and assaulting her private parts.The woman, Anju, a native of Mannathara, is currently undergoing treatment at Kollam District General Hospital.Chavara police have registered a case against her husband Nandu and his parents following her complaint.Anju and Nandu got married four months ago. She alleged that the harassment began within a week of the marriage, when her husband's family allegedly complained that the dowry brought by her was insufficient.About a month after the wedding, Nandu left for Saudi Arabia and later took Anju there.According to Anju, the abuse intensified after they reached Saudi Arabia.She alleged that Nandu frequently assaulted her using objects available at home, including a pressure cooker, stone and laptop charger cables. She suffered a serious head injury after allegedly being struck with a pressure cooker.She also alleged that Nandu kicked her in the abdomen and subjected her to brutal assault on her private parts. The woman has multiple injury marks on her body, which she said were caused by repeated assaults.Apart from the physical abuse, Anju alleged that she was subjected to severe psychological harassment.She said Nandu threatened her with a knife and forced her to record voice messages making derogatory statements about herself. She said she was even forced to record a statement saying she wanted to work in a sex racket after divorcing him.Anju said she was brought back to Kerala following the alleged abuse and was subsequently able to seek medical treatment and approach the police.She alleged that details of the assault, particularly the attacks on her abdomen and private parts, were not properly recorded when police took her statement at the hospital.Meanwhile, the police have began the investigation.Stay updated with the latest Thiruvananthapuram news. articles.title: Will Brazil’s Lula halt the right-wing wave sweeping Latin America?
articles.summary: Lula has remained a symbol for much of the global left amid the rise of the far right in Latin America.
articles.body:
Brazil votes on Sunday in a presidential election that pits President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against far-right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro. Will the left-wing incumbent be able to prevent Brazil from joining Latin America’s shift to the right?

A wave of right-wing election victories in recent years, including in Colombia, Chile and Argentina, has swept Latin America, aided by United States President Donald Trump’s administration under a new framework he calls the “Donroe Doctrine”, an updated version of the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine, aimed at restoring the pre-eminence of the United States in the Western Hemisphere.

Lula has sought to portray Senator Bolsonaro, whom he has called a “nobody” in campaign speeches, as a stand-in for a broader right-wing movement spreading across Latin America.

As Brazil heads to the polls, will Lula be able to halt the right-wing wave in the region?

Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva , better known simply as Lula, is the current president and the candidate for the Workers’ Party, or the PT.

The 80-year-old has been a central figure in Brazilian politics for decades, serving two four-year presidential terms between 2003 and 2011, and is currently serving his third term, which began in 2023.

His time in office has been defined by an effort to boost democracy, which was restored after a US-backed military dictatorship ruled the country for decades until the 1980s. He introduced a series of social programmes meant to address inequality, helping lift millions out of poverty.

Lula has also sought to forge ties between developing, non-Western countries on the global stage .

“He has come to embody the institutionalisation and consolidation of Brazilian democracy since the end of the dictatorship,” Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and the author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera in a phone call.

The 45-year-old has emerged as the heir to his father’s position as leader of Brazil’s political right and Lula’s main challenger. He is running as the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party.

Flavio Bolsonaro has pledged a hard stance on crime and violence and close collaboration with the Trump administration, which has designated several criminal groups in Brazil as “terrorist organisations”.

He has also promised to rein in inflation and government spending, with an adviser stating that he would implement a debt ceiling if elected.

Flavio has also sought to turn his father’s conviction into a story of political persecution, denouncing his trial as illegitimate and seeking his release from prison.

“I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro, so that he may place the presidential sash across my chest,” he said at a campaign event in September.

“The Bolsonaro family’s pitch is that the institutions that Brazilian democracy has erected since the end of dictatorship are either rotten and unresponsive, and that we need a sharp turn away from this status quo,” Pagliarini said.

“The stakes of this election are incredibly stark because the candidates stand for such opposing visions about what Brazil’s recent history means,” he added.

A series of polls on Saturday suggested that Lula is slightly ahead of Senator Bolsonaro.

The polls have projected the race to be close, with a likely run-off between the left-wing incumbent and his far-right challenger.

A poll by CNT/MDA, a prominent political opinion and electoral poll in Brazil, gave Lula 47.3 percent while Bolsonaro trailed at 43.1 percent. MDA surveyed 2,007 people from September 30 to October 2, with an estimated margin of error of 2.2 percentage points.

According to Datafolha, which surveyed 4,006 people on October 2-3 with a margin of error of 2 percentage points, in a run-off, Lula would get 47 percent and Bolsonaro 46 percent.

Polls suggested Bolsonaro was favoured over Lula on issues of inflation, combating corruption, and crime and drug trafficking, while Lula was seen more favourably on issues of poverty and inequality, foreign affairs and healthcare.

If no candidate wins more than 50 percent of Sunday’s valid votes – which exclude blank and null ballots – the two frontrunners advance to a run-off on October 25.

Can Lula halt the right-wing wave in Latin America?

In 2023, when Lula returned to power in Brazil, he remained a symbol for much of the global left, attracting visitors ranging from former Uruguayan President Pepe Mujica to the philosopher Noam Chomsky.

He was also convinced that Brazil stood on the front line of a broader struggle against a global right-wing movement.

The January 8, 2023, attacks by Bolsonaro supporters on government buildings in Brasilia, days after Lula’s inauguration, only reinforced that belief for many.

But Lula’s government still struggles with voter frustration over rising living costs, and it has not overcome the polarisation that has gripped the country for nearly a decade.

Moreover, while Lula has revived Brazil’s leadership role in the BRICS bloc, boosted ties with countries like China and expanded engagement with Europe, recent right-wing victories in South America, and a confrontational relationship with the Trump administration have left him increasingly isolated in the Western Hemisphere.

Some Brazilian diplomats said Washington views the country as the last big obstacle to a sweep of Trump-aligned governments across Latin America, after recent victories in Chile, Colombia, Honduras and Peru, and an unprecedented expansion of US power in Venezuela after its military intervention.

In Washington, progressives view Lula as a “beacon of hope”, Alex Main of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a left-leaning think tank, told the Reuters news agency.

In neighbouring Argentina, opponents of libertarian President Javier Milei see Lula’s possible re-election as a boost before next year’s vote.

“If Lula wins, it will create a countercurrent to what has been taking hold in the region and show there is resistance to these right-wing winds,” Santiago Cafiero, a congressman and former foreign minister, told Reuters.

Diplomats from liberal governments in Europe who have been supportive of Brazil’s progressive climate initiatives are also watching closely.

“If human rights are being violated in a pretty big way or if the Amazon is being deforested in a big way, then it’s going to be much more difficult for us to engage with Brazil,” a European ambassador, who asked not to be named, said.

But Lula has remained steadfast in his campaigns.

“As long as I am alive, the far right will not return to power in this country,” he has repeatedly said.

Fernando Brancoli, an associate professor of international security and geopolitics at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, said a win for Lula or Bolsonaro is going to change the direction of the whole continent.

“Brazil is the last progressive or left-wing bastion right now, so whoever is going to win will shift Brazil’s foreign policy, and this is going to have an atmospheric consequence end of the day,” he told Al Jazeera.

Could foreign interference impact the presidential race?

As with many recent elections across the region, corruption and concerns about US intervention in the country’s domestic affairs loom over the campaign and Lula’s efforts to quash the right-wing wave.

The US president has frequently threatened to cut off economic assistance to Latin American countries if his preferred candidate fails to win. Trump had also used sanctions to target members of the Brazilian judiciary involved in the case against the elder Bolsonaro, which he portrayed as a “witch-hunt”. Trump also placed heavy tariffs on Brazil in a bid to have the case thrown out.

Lula’s government denied visas to two US officials who sought to travel to Brazil, saying they planned to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazilian elections. Lula’s government has warned the US against meddling in the country’s domestic affairs.

Trump has himself used false claims of rampant fraud to justify efforts to remain in office despite his election loss in 2020.

A group of 31 Democratic US Congress members recently sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticising “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazilian elections.

Reuters reported that Brazilian intelligence officials also briefed a French and German delegation in September about possible interference in the election by outside powers such as the US and Russia. The officials said US interference ranged “from lawfare to interference that is openly acknowledged”.

Brancoli said that for the first time in Brazil’s modern history, the US has made an explicit move to try to change the direction of the election.

He said Brazil is the most heavily tariffed country by the US at more than 50 percent. “And Trump has said that he’s doing those taxes not because of trade reasons but because of political reasons,” he told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Ethiopian government forces seize Tigray capital Mekelle as TPLF withdraws
articles.summary: Federal troops and allied fighters seen in control of the city after capturing main regional airport.
articles.body:
The group leading an armed Ethiopian opposition alliance says it has withdrawn from Mekelle, the capital of the northern region of Tigray, after an advance by government forces and allied fighters.

In a statement on social media late on Saturday, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) said it had “temporarily moved out of Mekelle” to “operate from somewhere else”.

The announcement came hours after Ethiopia’s federal army and pro-government fighters recaptured Mekelle’s main airport. A source close to the Tigray Peace Forces, a pro-government militia, ‌told the Reuters news agency its fighters had entered Mekelle’s centre on Saturday afternoon, followed by the Ethiopian military.

A humanitarian source and a Mekelle resident who asked not to be named confirmed the city was under the control of government forces, Reuters reported on Sunday.

Separately, a humanitarian source also told the AFP news agency that staff on the ground said the TPLF had abandoned the regional capital. “Ethiopian federal forces and allied forces have reportedly been observed in Mekelle city … across various locations,” the source said.

Fighting broke out on September 23 after seven armed and political groups announced an alliance aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establishing an inclusive transitional administration.

The return of the hostilities followed the collapse of a 2022 peace deal that ended a devastating war between the federal government and forces from Tigray.

The latest round of violence is also leading to fears of a wider war that draws in other countries in the region.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing the opposition coalition.

Khartoum and Cairo have denied involvement. Eritrea, which fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal army in the 2020-2022 war, severed diplomatic ties with Ethiopia over the accusations.

Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi appeared to reference the conflict ahead of a meeting with leaders of Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan on Sunday, saying cross-border challengers require “dialogue, not confrontation”.

Addressing the African Union’s mid-year coordination summit in Egypt’s coastal town of El-Alamein, el-Sisi said Egypt opposed foreign interference in African states and called for relations to be based on “mutual respect, good neighbourliness, dialogue and consultation, far from unilateral policies or narrow interests”.

On Saturday, the United States urged Ethiopia and Eritrea “to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors, exercise maximum restraint and return to dialogue and cooperation”.

In a statement, the US Department of State warned that the increasing tensions “have the potential to affect the entire region”.

The TPLF began as an armed movement against Ethiopia’s military government in the 1970s. It later became the dominant force in a coalition that governed Ethiopia for nearly three decades until 2018 when Abiy came into office.

Relations between Abiy’s government and the TPLF deteriorated until war broke out in November 2020. The fighting killed hundreds of thousands of people, forced millions from their homes and largely cut off Tigray from the rest of the world.

articles.title: Purchase of field in Jersey aims to expand 'green lung'
articles.summary: It is hoped the prospective sale provides a haven for wildlife in an urban area.
articles.body:
Conservationists have said they are planning to buy a field to extend a "green lung" in one of Jersey's most built-up parishes.

The National Trust for Jersey said it had secured the rights to acquire the land near Maupertuis Farm in St Clement and hoped to complete the purchase shortly.

A green lung is an area of fields, parkland or vegetation within an otherwise urban area, providing space for wildlife and helping to reduce pollution.

The trust previously raised £50,000 in 37 days to buy a nearby field on Samares Lane in 2021.

The trust said the latest acquisition would help preserve the agricultural heritage of Maupertuis Farm and the surrounding area.

Chief executive Alan Le Maistre said green spaces were becoming "ever more precious" and protecting them was particularly important in densely developed parts of the island.

"It is a privilege to have the opportunity to extend this green lung for both the wildlife and people of the area," he said.

The National Trust for Jersey, which celebrated its 90th anniversary in August , manages about 1,800 vergées of land across the island.

It invited people who want to support the latest acquisition to contact the charity directly.

articles.title: Iran says Hormuz to remain closed until US meets conditions
articles.summary: Tehran says reopening Strait of Hormuz has been its main goal, while the US continues to focus on nuclear talks.
articles.body:
The Strait of Hormuz is going to remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker has said.

Iranian state-linked news agency Nournews, quoting ⁠Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, reported on Sunday that Washington made “some proposals through a mediator” days after the US replied ⁠to Iran’s diplomatic proposal.

The US should know “that the era of wasting time and dictating unilateral demands is over”, Ghalibaf said, adding Iran’s position remains “clear and definite”.

He emphasised that “the Strait of Hormuz will not open until our seven conditions based on the Islamabad memorandum are met”, and that Iran is “present on the military battlefield and will confront them with new surprises”.

He added that Iran was neither “excited” nor “intimidated” by the latest US proposals and would “both fight and negotiate”.

US President Donald Trump ruled out an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz last week, hours after Iran put forward a roadmap to reopening the strait, through which one-fifth of global oil and natural gas is shipped during peacetime.

Last month, Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran in his speech on the floor of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).

On Sunday, Iranian Foreign ⁠Minister Abbas Araghchi also said Iran is “serious about finding diplomatic solutions just as we are serious about defending ourselves”.

Speaking to foreign ambassadors and diplomats in Tehran, Araghchi said Iran had clearly explained ⁠its conditions for reopening the strait and ⁠that Tehran hoped Washington would choose diplomacy and accept its proposal.

However, Araghchi warned that if the US takes military action again, Iran is “more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves”.

Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei added that Tehran used the UNGA platform last month to provide world leaders with its position on ending the US-Israel war on Iran.

He said the US has continued to focus on nuclear talks , while reopening the strait has been Iran’s main goal.

“We are at this stage mainly focusing on the strait, and our principal concern is to reach a solution and to have peace and stability restored within this waterway,” Baghaei said.

The Strait of Hormuz has been largely blocked and disrupted for more than seven months, since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, driving one of the worst maritime shipping disruptions in decades.

articles.title: Brazil votes in deeply polarised election pitting Lula against Bolsonaro
articles.summary: Close race expected as left-wing leader Lula seeks fourth nonconsecutive term against right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro.
articles.body:
Polls have opened in Brazil’s presidential election , once again pitting left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against a right-wing candidate from the Bolsonaro family – Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

About 160 million registered voters are eligible to cast ballots in Sunday’s elections, which will elect lawmakers, governors and senators.

If no presidential candidate wins more than 50 percent of valid votes, the top two contenders will proceed to a run-off on October 25.

Most opinion polls ahead of the vote showed a close contest, with Lula holding a marginal advantage over Bolsonaro that tightens further in a potential second round.

Flavio Bolsonaro voted in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday, telling reports he wants to “free the Brazilian people”.

“Brazil needs change … it cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed,” he said, adding that he was confident of victory in the first round.

Lula, of the Workers’ Party, is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term. The 80-year-old, who previously served as president from 2003 to 2010, wants to continue his series of social programmes aimed at addressing inequality.

Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party, has promised a hard stance on crime and insecurity. The 45-year-old has also pledged close collaboration with the United States under President Donald Trump.

His father is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence over his role in a coup plot following his election loss to Lula by 1.8 percentage points in 2022. The far-right leader’s conviction and that of several military officers raised questions about the strength of Brazilian democracy, reviving past traumas of the 21-year-long period during which Brazil was ruled by a US-backed military dictatorship.

Reporting from Sao Paulo, Al Jazeera’s Lucia Newman, said “the Brazilian president is on a collision course with Donald Trump, who is a vocal and ardent supporter of Lula’s longtime foe, Jair Bolsonaro”.

“That puts Brazil in the middle of a fierce competition between Washington and China for political, diplomatic, and economic dominance, especially since Brazil is a powerhouse on all these fronts,” Newman added.

The presidential election has been dominated by issues such as crime, insecurity and the high cost of living. Corruption and concerns about US intervention in the country’s domestic affairs have also loomed over the campaign.

A recent survey by Quaest says violence was cited as the biggest concern by 31 percent of respondents, followed by corruption (20 percent), economy (19 percent) and healthcare (12 percent).

“The stakes of this election are incredibly stark because the candidates stand for such opposing visions about what Brazil’s recent history means”, Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and the author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera .

He added that while Lula embodies the “consolidation of Brazilian democracy since the end of the dictatorship”, the Bolsonaro family argues that “the institutions that Brazilian democracy has erected since the end of dictatorship are either rotten and unresponsive”.

articles.title: 'Not a single post, statement': BJP launches blistering attack on Congress over Captain Smit Machchhar
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Sunday accused the Congress leadership of maintaining “silence” over Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar, who was seriously injured
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Sunday accused the Congress leadership of maintaining “silence” over Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar, who was seriously injured after his Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked him in the cockpit of a Dubai-Tel Aviv flydubai flight, while also targeting the opposition party over its latest appointments in Uttar Pradesh.Addressing reporters, BJP spokesperson and Rajya Sabha MP Sudhanshu Trivedi said the incident was an occasion of national pride and questioned why senior Congress leaders had not publicly acknowledged Machchhar's brave actions.“For India, this is an occasion of great pride, but there are also some occasions that are a matter of shame. Not a single word, not a single post, and not a single press statement has come from the Congress family for Captain Smit Machchhar. This raises a serious question,” Trivedi said.Machchhar was attacked on Wednesday aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, which was carrying 174 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Despite being seriously injured, he managed to open the cockpit door, allowing others to intervene and helping prevent the aircraft from being brought down. The plane was subsequently diverted safely to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.Also Read| ‘Free the terrorist’: Passengers claim flydubai crew told them to release co-pilot after attack - reportTrivedi contrasted the Congress leadership's alleged silence with the response from Prime Minister Narendra Modi and leaders abroad, who praised Machchhar act of bravery.The BJP leader then turned his criticism towards Sonia Gandhi, Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, alleging that the party's political calculations had influenced its response.“Rahul Gandhi, the ‘wayward prince’ of the Gandhi family who was once so distressed over Gaza, seems to be so ‘terrified of the vote bank’ that he is not able to utter a single word to hail the valour of Machchhar,” Trivedi said.He also accused the Congress of “silent support to terrorism” and demanded that its top leadership explain its position.Trivedi linked the attack to the Congress's recent organisational changes in Uttar Pradesh. On Friday, the party appointed Aradhana Mishra-Mona as state Congress president and Saharanpur MP Imran Masood as working president, replacing Ajay Rai as the state chief.“On the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, who is a symbol of peace and non-violence, Congress has appointed Imran Masood, who is infamous for his remark that he will ‘chop Modi into pieces’, as the party's Uttar Pradesh unit working president,” Trivedi said.He also alleged that Mishra had previously stopped party workers from raising the “Bharat Mata ki Jai” slogan.“This demonstrates how vast the gap has become between Mahatma Gandhi and the Gandhis of today,” he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Germany’s Friedrich Merz arrives in Kyiv to the sound of sirens and explosions
articles.summary: KYIV — The sound of air raid sirens and explosions rang out in Ukraine’s capital Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, pledging support for Ukraine and urging Russia to halt its ⁠escalating attacks.
articles.body: KYIV — The sound of air raid sirens and explosions rang out in Ukraine’s capital Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, pledging support for Ukraine and urging Russia to halt its ⁠escalating attacks. Merz will announce a package of measures including the release of €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid and €350 million for repairs in the energy sector, German government officials said. A deal for joint production of various kinds of drones is also due to be finalised. The two leaders visited the badly damaged building of Ukraine’s Academy of Sciences, where at least two people died in a drone strike last week as Russia pounded ⁠the heart of Kyiv with some of the most persistent drone strikes ​since ⁠the start of the war in 2022. “I can only repeat it once again from this point: Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war,” Merz said. “We are ready for talks, we are ready to discuss bringing this ⁠war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop,” he added. Four air ​raid alerts ⁠were heard across the capital on Sunday morning, and ‌explosions and air defence systems also sounded across the city. One of the Russian strikes hit the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, damaging its roadway, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. He said the strike had injured two people and damaged ‌a hot water supply system in the area. Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s ‌bridges since last week in an effort to disrupt links between the capital’s two banks and logistics routes between central and eastern Ukraine. Merz seeks progress on reforms Merz is accompanied on the visit by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and an economic delegation including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence, Quantum Systems and other companies. Merz ⁠is also expected to press the Ukrainian government for progress on reforms requested by E.U. partners, including in the fight against corruption. Zelenskyy said on Wednesday, after speaking to Merz by phone, that Ukraine would soon finalise a deal with Germany for the production of drones, missiles and related software. A key focus of the agreement is expected to be the rapid production of anti-jet drones, which Quantum, a German defence-technology company, has successfully tested. Since the summer, Russia has used dozens of high-speed jet attack drones daily to target civilian and military infrastructure. In April, Quantum and Ukrainian manufacturer WIY Drones announced the creation of Quantum WIY Industries, a joint venture ‌to produce the Strila interceptor drone and related air-defence technologies. Long-range weapons The deal also involves the ​joint development and production of weapons with a range of more than 1,000 km (600 miles) that Ukraine can use ‌to launch attacks deep inside Russia. Russia’s Foreign Ministry said ⁠on Saturday that Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in Ukraine in what it said were retaliatory strikes ⁠for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months. It warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against staying in or travelling to Ukraine. Zelenskyy told Reuters on Saturday his ‌country’s armed forces would double down on ​their attacks on oil refineries in Russia in response to Moscow’s “new ‌doctrine” of escalating attacks on civilian infrastructure, which he said ​was aimed at forcing residents of Kyiv and other cities to flee.
