articles.title: Sharmila Mona Sinha: The third daughter who turned deficit into dividend and became a US Hall of Famer
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: As a little girl growing up in Calcutta, Sharmila Mona Sinha was often reminded of a familiar Indian “disappointment”:
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: As a little girl growing up in Calcutta, Sharmila Mona Sinha was often reminded of a familiar Indian “disappointment”: she was the third daughter. In a society where the arrival of a son was treated as a family dividend and another daughter as a deficit, she absorbed the message early and decided to do something about it. “I wanted to be a boy and do what boys did,” she recalled.Last week, the Kolkata-born daughter entered the National Women’s Hall of Fame in Seneca Falls, New York - the cradle of the American women’s-rights movement - becoming only the second woman of Indian origin to receive the honour, after former PepsiCo CEO Indra Nooyi. It is a fitting destination for a woman whose journey has taken her from Kolkata to Smith College, Wall Street, corporate America and, ultimately, the global campaign for women’s equality.Sinha’s journey did not begin with grand ambitions of changing the world; it began with family, expectations and an encounter with poverty that left a lasting impression. As a volunteer at a Mother Teresa orphanage in Kolkata, what struck her was not simply the deprivation around her but something more unsettling: the orphanage had few boys because, she was told, abandoned boys were more readily adopted. Even among abandoned children, gender could determine who got a second chance.Another influence came closer to home. Only in her teens did she learn that her grandmother had helped organise women during India’s freedom movement. The discovery gave her a sense that challenging the status quo was not alien to her family. “I don’t receive this extraordinary honor as mine alone. I receive it as a fistful of rice, placed in my hands with a responsibility to pass it on,” she said in her induction speech, recalling how her mother in Kolkata set aside a fistful of rice each morning for someone in greater need.At 18, she left India for Smith College in Massachusetts, graduating in economics and art history before earning an MBA from Columbia Business School. She entered Wall Street as an investment banker at Morgan Stanley and later moved into corporate America, working for companies including Procter & Gamble, Unilever and Elizabeth Arden. It was a world of balance sheets, brands, mergers and markets -- seemingly far removed from the women’s-rights movement.Over time, however, Sinha began wondering whether the tools she had acquired in business could be deployed for a different kind of return. Rather than abandoning the language of capital, management, and organisational efficiency, she brought it into philanthropy and social change.She became a leader of Women Moving Millions, a network of women philanthropists whose members have committed roughly $1 billion to organisations working for women and girls. She co-founded Raising Change, which helps social-impact organisations strengthen fundraising and organisational capacity, and helped establish the Asian Women’s Leadership University. At Smith, her alma mater, she became a trustee and helped lead the Women for the World campaign, which raised approximately $486 million.Her portfolio eventually expanded beyond philanthropy. Sinha became an executive producer of documentaries, including the Oscar-nominated To Kill a Tiger, while also supporting the campaign for the Equal Rights Amendment and the planned Smithsonian American Women’s History Museum. Since 2022, she has served as CEO of Equality Now, the international organisation working to eliminate discriminatory laws affecting women and girls. Her work now takes her into the harder terrain of changing laws and legal systems, addressing issues from child marriage and sexual violence to women’s economic rights.Sinha’s story offers an unusually Indian lesson about the evolution of feminism. She did not begin by marching in the streets; she began as a daughter in a Kolkata household, went to an American women’s college, entered investment banking, learned corporate strategy and eventually turned those skills toward changing institutions. Her Hall of Fame induction is therefore more than another accolade for a prominent philanthropist. It is a long-distance answer to the question that confronted the little girl in Calcutta: What might that “wrong” daughter become if nobody put a ceiling on her?Four decades later, the answer has been inscribed in the National Women’s Hall of Fame. And alongside it is an increasingly familiar Indian-American footnote: after Indra Nooyi, another daughter of India has entered America’s pantheon of women leaders.You use AI every day. articles.title: Co-pilot accused of trying to hijack Flydubai plane probably acted alone, Israeli sources say
articles.summary: The co-pilot accused of attacking his colleague on board the Flydubai flight to Israel and trying to seize the controls probably acted alone, Israeli sources told CNN.
articles.body: The co-pilot accused of attacking his colleague on board the Flydubai flight to Israel and trying to seize the controls probably acted alone, Israeli sources told CNN. International investigators are still working to determine a motive but an Israeli official said information from the inquiry suggested the suspect acted alone. Another Israeli source said that, at the moment, Israel does not know of any link to a group or government. Both stressed this was their understanding so far. The United Arab Emirates and Israel are both investigating the incident. The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing, is also conducting investigations. The attorney general of the UAE, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said the co-pilot on board the flight had attempted to seize control of the plane by attacking his colleague with a crash ax – a piece of equipment required on most aircraft. The attorney general called the attempted hijacking a “terrorist act.” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday that Israel understands the suspect “underwent Islamist radical indoctrination,” based on “personal information” collected during the suspect’s ongoing questioning. Netanyahu did not give any further details. In the immediate aftermath of the attack, US President Donald Trump said that the suspect could be linked to Iran “based on what I’m hearing.” But he gave no other details. Flydubai flight FZ1073 narrowly avoided disaster on its journey from Dubai, plummeting thousands of feet in a matter of minutes amid the attack on the plane’s captain. Despite being wounded, pilot Captain Smit Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door and signal his distress to passengers and crew, who bravely rushed into the cockpit to regain control of the aircraft. Sources told CNN the suspect, named as Hamam al-Hammami, is an Omani national who had been removed from a previous job at Oman’s national airline last year following concerns about his extremist views. A LinkedIn profile bearing the name Hamam al-Hammami said he worked at Oman Air for seven years, leaving in February 2025, before joining the Moroccan airline Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and departing in January 2026. One source told CNN that the profile belongs to the Flydubai pilot in Wednesday’s incident. The profile has since been deleted and CNN has reached out to LinkedIn for comment. A post made to the LinkedIn profile on Wednesday, about nine hours after the incident, included a photo of the former leader of al Qaeda. It is unclear who published the posts or whether they were scheduled in advance. An Israeli official told CNN that al-Hammami had worked for Flydubai for only eight months. Another source said the alleged assailant had previously worked for Royal Air Maroc. In a statement to the Associated Press, Air Maroc said the suspect trained with the airline for three months in 2025 as part of the pre-employment process but he was not selected. The Australian Federal Police (AFP) also told CNN that it is investigating al-Hammami’s links to the country, and said an update will be provided when appropriate.

articles.title: Yemen’s leader announces military operation to retake Houthi-held territory
articles.summary: Rashad al-Alimi says the campaign aims to restore state authority throughout Yemen.
articles.body:
⁠The ⁠Saudi Arabia-backed head of ⁠Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, ⁠Rashad al-Alimi, has announced the start of military operations to retake the ⁠remaining territory held by ⁠the Iran-backed Houthi armed group ⁠and restore ⁠state ⁠authority across the country.

In a televised address, al-Alimi said on Sunday the internationally recognised government’s forces would extend “the authority of the state and its institutions over the entire national territory”.

“We have instructed the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned tasks under an approved plan until the country is liberated from the Houthis,” he said.

Al-Alimi added that all state institutions will be placed on full alert “until the mission is completed and victory is achieved”.

The development comes after Yemeni forces “executed 257 precision targeting operations ” against Houthi sites, movements, and military capabilities on Saturday, according to the spokesman for Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces, Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili.

He added that initial estimates indicate that the operations killed at least 700 Houthi rebels.

The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition supporting the government, Turki al-Malik, said on Saturday that the Houthis’ “ties to external agendas” have brought “chaos and devastation to Yemen”.

Early on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said its armed forces carried out 97 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi reinforcements on the Tor al-Baha front and the Taiz axis, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.

Later in the day, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree later claimed the group’s forces had fired ballistic missiles and drones at two Saudi Aramco sites in Saudi Arabia – one in Riyadh and the other in the area of Khurais, some 150km (93 miles) north-east of the capital.

There was no immediate comment by Saudi Arabia.

The fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July, displacing hundreds of thousands of people since.

In mid-September, the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital route for global oil shipments, before anti-Houthi forces stabilised front lines.

Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, forcing the Yemeni government to retreat to Aden.

articles.title: Yemen leader announces major military operations against Iran-backed Houthis
articles.summary: ADEN— The leader of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government announced the beginning of a major military operation against the ⁠Iran-backed Houthis on Sunday, aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
articles.body: ADEN— The leader of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government announced the beginning of a major military operation against the ⁠Iran-backed Houthis on Sunday, aimed at seizing the territory under their control. Regional and western officials had previously told Reuters that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground. “Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the ⁠republic and extend the authority of the state and its ​institutions ⁠across the entire national territory,” Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address. Saudi Arabia entered neighbouring Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of ⁠the internationally recognised government, which the Houthis had driven out of the capital Sanaa. A truce agreed between the ​warring parties ⁠in 2022 largely held until this year, when ‌the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war. Houthis’ lightning offensive Despite the preparations for a counteroffensive, the Houthis have so far maintained the initiative on ‌the ground, weeks after seizing the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait in ‌a lightning offensive down the coast that saw government forces collapse. Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, ⁠which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict. In the last 48 hours, the Houthis have made gains against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Yemen’s Taiz, military sources said, advancing on the last road between the city and Aden, where the Saudi-backed Yemeni government is based. Houthi control over the Taiz-Aden road would lead to an effective siege of the city, Yemen’s third-largest, inhabited by hundreds of thousands of civilians and where thousands of government forces are also stationed. It would also consolidate control of that flat coastal Bab el-Mandeb area by seizing ‌the rugged mountains overlooking them in the western Taiz countryside, according to Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a veteran ​Yemeni journalist from Taiz now working as a political analyst. “This will help them protect their ‌back in case of any operation against the coastline, ⁠and make recapturing those areas much more difficult,” he said. The city is important not just for ⁠its strategic location; Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi is from the region, and a siege of Taiz would amplify an already-dire humanitarian situation in the ‌country. Three-in-four families in parts of ​Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge ‌in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands ​of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week.

articles.title: In 2012, a retired FBI agent began searching for ‘lost’ apples; more than a decade later, his mission has helped rediscover 30 forgotten varieties across the Pacific Northwest
articles.summary: Retirement from the FBI gave Washington native Dave Benscoter plenty of time on his hands in 2012.
articles.body: Retirement from the FBI gave Washington native Dave Benscoter plenty of time on his hands in 2012. Little did he know that a routine day of yard work would eventually lead him on a more than decade-long quest to rediscover apples that had all but vanished from the Pacific Northwest.Benscoter was helping a fellow parishioner from his church with some yard work when he noticed something unusual about the apple trees in her orchard. The varieties looked unlike any apples he had encountered before.“So I gave her a call, and I said, ‘Do you know what kind of apple trees are in your orchard?’” Benscoter recalled during an appearance on the Evergreen Thumb podcast last November.The woman could identify some of the trees. “And she said, ‘Well, I know the very top ones were named Yellow Transparent. They’re the very first apple that ripens in the year, in July.’”Another row contained Wealthy apples, an older variety notable for being the first apple ever bred in the United States. But beyond those, the identity of the remaining trees remained a mystery.“But she didn’t know the rest of the apples,” Benscoter said. “So I jumped online, and I just basically started going down rabbit holes.”From FBI agent to ‘apple detective’That internet search soon developed into an unlikely obsession. Benscoter began researching apple varieties that had once been cultivated across the Pacific Northwest but were increasingly difficult to find. He searched through nature studies, family recipes, county fair newspapers and other historical records, looking for clues that could lead him to what enthusiasts call “lost apples.”His search eventually brought him together with Joanie Cooper and Sean Shepherd of Oregon’s Temperate Orchard Conservancy. The two, who Benscoter describes as “apple identification experts,” helped analyze the DNA of unusual specimens and determine their identities.“The first year we found one — it was the Fall Jenneting,” Benscoter said. “Now we have found 30 once-lost varieties.”The discoveries did not stop there. Along with his friend E.J. Brandt, Benscoter created the Lost Apple Project, turning their retirement years into a mission to locate and preserve historic apple trees.Since 2012, the two have searched eastern Washington, western Idaho and northern Oregon for apple trees dating back to before 1920.Preserving apples that history nearly forgotThe Lost Apple Project is not simply about finding unusual fruit. The nonprofit also works to ensure that rediscovered varieties survive for future generations.Brandt and Benscoter search for rare trees, collect apple specimens during the fall and have them identified. During winter, they return to the orchards to graft branches and propagate the varieties, helping grow new “heritage” trees.Their discoveries have included varieties with names as unusual as the apples themselves, including the Streaked Pippin, Sary Sinap and Nero.But one particular discovery has remained especially memorable for Benscoter because of the personal connection behind it.He recalled a farmer in Arkansas who had spent years hoping to find a Kittageskee apple, a variety that had once been grown in the state but had disappeared.“10 years ago, he was going to be retiring soon, and his one regret was that he had spent his whole life hoping to come across the Kittageskee [apple] that was grown in Arkansas, and unfortunately, he’d never found it,” Benscoter said.Then, roughly two years later, the search produced an unexpected breakthrough. Benscoter and his team found Kittageskee apples in southern Idaho.“The Lost Apple Project has members down in the Boise area, and somebody picked those apples and sent them in. I know it made him incredibly happy,” Benscoter said.“It was an apple that he thought he’d never be able to taste, and so that kind of stands out for me.”For Benscoter, what began as curiosity during a day of post-retirement yard work has grown into a long-running conservation effort. His journey from FBI agent to apple hunter has helped bring forgotten varieties back into the spotlight, and, in some cases, back onto people's tables.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
articles.summary: The Tory leader seeks to echo Margaret Thatcher as she sets out her guiding political principles.
articles.body:
Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and a 100 page statement on her guiding principles.

"I believe in common sense, people working hard and being rewarded for that effort," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.

She added that welfare should be a "safety net, not a lifestyle".

The Tory leader is trying to ensure her party stands out in a crowded political field. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in the opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, has characterised Reform leader Nigel Farage as a "grumpy grandpa" and she told Laura Kuenssberg that Labour leader Andy Burnham is "the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes".

She described herself as a "no-nonsense mum".

Asked if her plan for benefit cuts and a massive increase in prison places was a return to the "nasty party" of the past, she said: "It's the common sense party. That's what we're doing.

"And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?"

In her essay The Right Way - a deliberate echo of an essay written by Margaret Thatcher in 1976 entitled The Right Approach - Badenoch says the last Conservative government failed because it did not know what it stood for.

Despite the party's rhetoric during its 14 years in power, she said: "We did little to reverse the structural changes Labour had made which took the country in the wrong direction.

"The result was that the state grew by stealth."

The essay says the "next Conservative government will have one central principle: business, not government, creates growth".

The Tories would achieve growth through tax cuts, cutting red tape and reducing the size of the civil service back to pre-pandemic levels, the essay says.

And it adds: "What is really missing from politics and government today is people prepared to say no.

"Political parties now need to recruit those who have the stomach to say no to good causes when the resources simply are not there to do everything."

As their conference gets under way in Birmingham the Conservatives have pledged to end a childcare "cliff edge", which currently means parents earning more than £100,000 do not qualify for the entitlement.

The party has also promised to deliver 50,000 new prison places by slashing the overseas aid budget to £1bn a year in a bid to end the early release of offenders.

Over the 14 years the Conservatives were in power, around 500 net prison places were created, which takes into account 14,142 added in existing and new jails, set against 13,660 lost mainly to dilapidation and closures.

Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said the Tory Party "is stuck in the past and remains completely out of touch with what people across Britain want to see".

"Last week Andy Burnham set out a plan to bring back hope to Britain. Kemi Badenoch wants to drag our country back to a politics that let so many people down over the past 40 years."

articles.title: Why is fighting intensifying in Yemen’s Taiz governorate?
articles.summary: Fighting escalates in Taiz governorate as Yemen’s government and Houthis battle for control of key strategic locations.
articles.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-backed Houthis are engaged in a fierce struggle for the Taiz governorate, a key strategic area in the southwest of the country.

Rashad al-Alimi, chief of the Saudi Arabia-backed Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced on Sunday the start of a major offensive against the Houthis to regain lost territory. It is expected that this will result in more battles around Taiz, already the site of some of the most recent fighting.

Observers and analysts say that the Houthis are trying to consolidate their gains after seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month. For the government, the battle for Taiz represents a strategic and existential struggle for control of the country.

Taiz governorate is Yemen’s most populous region, with nearly 4.5 million people. The flat western coastal region sits on the Red Sea and includes the port city of Mocha and the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait.

These coastal regions were captured by the Houthis in a surprise and lightning campaign in early September, raising fears the group could choke off international shipping through the strait. They were also key supply routes for Taiz.

Much of the governorate lies within Yemen’s highlands and remains contested between the two sides. The region’s capital, Taiz City, is nestled between a number of mountains and is under government control. It is one of Yemen’s most populous cities and a key source of legitimacy for the Yemeni government.

The governorate sits between Yemen’s Houthi-controlled north and the government-held south. The Houthi advance threatens to isolate government forces from Aden, the southern coastal town where key state institutions are based.

Ibrahim Jalal, a senior researcher and policy adviser, told Al Jazeera that Taiz is a city of huge social, political, economic and military importance for the whole of Yemen.

“The Houthi attempt to isolate and constrict the city seeks to secure their coastal Red Sea gains up to Bab al-Mandeb, as well as double down on pressure on Lahij, Aden and much of the south,” said Jalal.

“The Houthis seek to expand their territorial control at the moment along the former boundaries of northern Yemen, or to say, that they want to remove all little pockets of resistance to consolidate control.”

Taiz has been one of the most heavily contested cities in the war, beginning shortly after Houthi forces captured the capital Sanaa in September 2014.

Thousands of civilians have been killed in a devastating Houthi siege and assault on the city, with government forces driving back repeated assaults between 2015 and 2022.

Fighting has been focused on Jabal Han, a mountain overlooking Taiz from the west, as well as a key road into the city.

Control over this mountain would allow the Houthis to attack people and supplies entering Taiz City from the southwest, Saeed Thabet, head of Al Jazeera’s bureau in Yemen, said.

There has been no clear winner in the battle for Taiz so far, which observers have described as a stalemate.

Al Jazeera’s Mohammed al-Qadi, reporting from the city, said government forces have launched dozens of air strikes on Houthi bases and positions across Taiz in recent days.

Houthi fighters are trying to advance under cover of intense artillery, tank, mortar and Katyusha rocket fire into the city.

Artillery fire could be heard around Taiz as residents appealed to be evacuated, Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz City, said on Sunday.

On that day, local authorities reported that a shell had hit a residential area in Dhubab, killing a 14-day-old infant. Other attacks have wounded civilians.

Government forces are also shelling Houthi forces positioned around the city.

Face-to-face fighting has now reached the countryside on the outskirts of Taiz City. Residents are fighting on their own initiative against Houthi attempts to infiltrate villages and mountain areas around Taiz, a local source said.

The heaviest fighting is taking place at the western axis of the city, where government forces have mounted a fierce defence at Jabal Han.

On Sunday, Yemen’s government forces announced gains against the Houthis, saying they had captured several areas, including a fort in Samaa.

The military command in Taiz also claimed its forces had repelled Houthi attacks on Jabal Han, Hazran and other points west of Taiz City.

Yemeni military spokesman Majed al-Nuzaili said government forces had carried out dozens of operations using aircraft, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers, resulting in hundreds of Houthi casualties. Al Jazeera could not verify these claims.

In early September, the Houthis managed to expand their control over Yemen’s Red Sea coast with unexpected speed and limited resistance.

However, they have faced much fiercer fighting from government forces in Taiz.

One key reason for this is the cohesion between government forces and the local tribes. Al Jazeera’s Yasser Hassan reports that tribesmen took part in Sunday’s capture of the Samaa Fort.

How are civilians in Taiz being impacted?

The humanitarian cost of the renewed fighting in Taiz has already manifested in a refugee crisis with limited access to humanitarian goods and services.

There has also been an increase in civilian casualties. Since fighting escalated in early September, nearly 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen, most of them from Taiz governorate, according to Yemen’s Executive Unit for IDP Camps Management.

The closure of some major roads into Taiz City has raised fears of an impending humanitarian disaster.

The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the World Health Organization (WHO) have both warned that the fighting was putting Yemen’s fragile healthcare system in peril.

Al Jazeera’s Hassan described the humanitarian situation as “very difficult” after government forces decided to shut down all roads leading into the city out of fear of Houthi infiltration.

Before Mocha was taken over by Houthis, its port was a critical supply line from which food and aid were delivered to Taiz City.

The ongoing war has also devastated the country. Nearly half of Yemen’s 34 million population face acute food insecurity, according to the UN, with about half a million people suffering severe malnutrition.

articles.title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
articles.summary: Two residents in Mekelle tell the BBC pro-government forces have taken control of the city.
articles.body:
Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.

The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.

Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.

Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.

The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.

The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.

How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia

Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.

However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.

Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.

The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.

On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.

Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.

The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

articles.title: How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk?
articles.summary: Aviation security protocols under scrutiny after co-pilot accused of attempted axe attack aboard Flydubai flight.
articles.body:
A Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain with an emergency axe and attempting to seize control of the flight bound for Israel had previously been barred from flying over concerns about alleged “extremist” views, raising questions about how he was allowed to fly to Tel Aviv.

The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, according to multiple media reports.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has described the September 30 incident aboard Flight FZ1073 as an attempted “terrorist” operation .

But investigators are still working to establish the motive and whether anyone else was connected to the attack, which has raised concerns about pilot vetting and aviation security.

So, what security checks do pilots have to go through and how al-Hammami may have evaded background checks?

How did al-Hammami apparently pass the checks?

That is now one of the central questions facing investigators.

Al-Hammami had previously been barred from flying in Oman because of concerns that he had adopted “extremist” views and was instead moved to an administrative role at Oman Air, according to sources who spoke to the AP news agency.

A Gulf diplomat told AP that al-Hammami had undergone standard security checks before being hired. It wasn’t immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted.

The US-based network CNN reported that a LinkedIn profile bearing al-Hammami’s name said he had spent seven years at Oman Air before leaving in February 2025. The profile said he joined Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and left in January this year.

It is unclear what those alleged views were or whether Oman informed other countries or airlines about its concerns.

What background checks do commercial pilots go through?

Background checks for commercial pilots vary by airline and country, with no single global standard governing the process, an airline pilot and instructor told Al Jazeera.

The captain with an international airline who chose to remain anonymous said pilots are generally required to obtain aviation medical certification from the regulator in the country where they are licensed to fly.

In the UAE, that is overseen by the General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA), he said.

Some airlines also require prospective pilots to provide police clearance certificates from their country of residence as part of pre-employment screening, the pilot added.

One type of check is a Class 1 medical assessment, which typically examines areas including vision, hearing, cardiovascular and neurological health, as well as conditions that could cause sudden incapacitation.

When it comes to security checks, aviation rules require background checks for personnel who have unescorted access to security-restricted areas.

Psychological assessments, drug and alcohol testing and other evaluations may be required depending on the jurisdiction.

Israel has some of the world’s toughest aviation security measures.

As a result, questions have been raised over how the alleged attacker was allowed to operate a flight to Israel, despite reportedly being an Omani national and Oman having no diplomatic relations with Israel.

According to the Haaretz newspaper, Israeli authorities received the Flydubai flight’s crew and passenger lists before it departed. Under a law passed in 2023, airlines are required to provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, to Israel up to 48 hours before a flight.

The Israel Tax Authority confirmed to Haaretz that it had received the lists for the Flydubai flight. The media outlet reported that the information is also supposed to be available to Israeli security bodies, including the Mossad, police and Shin Bet, to identify people who may pose a security risk.

According to security sources who spoke to Haaretz, the Transportation Ministry’s Security Department and the Mossad are responsible for checking foreign flight crews and issuing alerts if concerns arise.

However, two security sources told Haaretz that while the Transportation Ministry holds responsibility “on paper”, it does not have its own intelligence capacity.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel has longstanding arrangements with foreign airlines aimed at preventing pilots who are nationals of countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from flying there.

Netanyahu has described what happened as a “loophole” and Israel says it will now strengthen its checks.

The UAE has not yet publicly established a motive or announced whether investigators believe al-Hammami acted alone.

UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Saturday that the latest ‘terrorist’ attack is a new warning that the region’s fight against “extremism” is not over.

“This underscores the importance of the UAE’s early and firm stance: no tolerance for extremism and no leniency towards its rhetoric. Security begins with confronting hatred and drying up the sources of extremism,” he posted on X.

articles.title: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues
articles.summary: Measures include extended opening hours, as well as an audio guide and additional seating for visitors.
articles.body:
The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.

The measures include plans for longer opening hours, as well as an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.

A museum spokesperson said the public response to the 11th Century embroidery had been "extraordinary", but acknowledged that some visitors had waited longer than they would have wanted.

Some people reported waits of up to two hours, while hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early last week due to a private event.

Some ticket holders took to social media to complain about the disruption.

One disappointed visitor said the trip had been a "big event" they had looked forward to, while another wrote she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux Tapestry, and bought tickets only to be turned away after queuing.

The museum later apologised to those who had been unable to enter and said they would be issued refunds and priority booking slots for a rearranged time.

From Monday, visitors will be offered an audio guide with more information about the embroidery, while additional signage and seating will be provided for those queuing to reach the main exhibition.

The museum said it planned to introduce longer opening hours to prevent queues building during the day and allow people with later bookings more time to view the exhibition.

Details of the extended hours have not yet been disclosed.

Demand for the exhibition has been high since tickets first went on sale in July, with a record 100,000 sold on the first day.

Members of the public who were not successful in the first ticket release will have two further chances to view the masterpiece when further tickets go on sale in October and January.

Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared with its usual €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy. Children under 16 can visit the London exhibition for free.

The exhibition opened on 10 September but has experienced a series of problems with queues and congestion, with some visitors spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry.

Visitors were later stopped from taking photographs and a recorded message was introduced encouraging people to continue moving through the one-way exhibition.

The 70m-long Bayeux Tapestry depicts 58 scenes outlining the extraordinary events surrounding the Norman conquest of England , the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and the end of Anglo-Saxon rule in Britain.

Despite its name, the work is an embroidery rather than a tapestry and contains approximately 626 human figures and 200 horses.

The Bayeux Tapestry is on loan from the French government, having been transported from its home in Normandy - where it has been exhibited since 1983. It will be on display until July 2027.

The loan marks the first time the tapestry has returned to the UK since it was created more than 900 years ago.

articles.title: India, UAE, Saudi, Israel, Oman and Australia: How 6 countries got caught up in flydubai terror
articles.summary: The stabbing on Indian pilot Smit Machchhar by Omani co-pilot Hammam al-Hammami on flydubai flight has now brought six countries officially into the fold.
articles.body: The stabbing on Indian pilot Smit Machchhar by Omani co-pilot Hammam al-Hammami on flydubai flight has now brought six countries officially into the fold. The attack on September 30 was on a flight flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, when it was forced to make an emergency landing after the stabbing of Indian pilot by his Omani co pilot.The incident unfolded on September 30 when flydubai Flight FZ1073, travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv with more than 170 people on board, went into a sharp descent after the co-pilot allegedly attacked Captain Smit Machchhar inside the cockpit. The jet plunged nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds amid the fight.Machchhar, an Indian national, managed to open the cockpit door despite being injured, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the co-pilot. The aircraft was diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely and the alleged attacker was detained. The UAE is doing the direct investigation, with Israel, and now Australia and other authorities also examining different aspects of the case.So, here's how 6 countries have gotten "mixed-up" in one incident.India: Pilot Smit Machchhar hailed as a heroIndia’s connection to the incident centres on Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot who was attacked by his Omani co-pilot while flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Despite being seriously injured, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the co-pilot and enabling two other pilots aboard the aircraft to take control. The plane was then safely landed in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.Machchhar’s actions drew praise from both Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. PM Modi called him a “hero” and said his courage helped save hundreds of lives and avert a major tragedy and even held a video call with him. Netanyahu also hailed Machchhar for saving the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and also called him while the pilot in recovering in Abu Dhabi hospital. Indian authorities in Saudi Arabia have been assisting Machchhar and his family, while he has been recovering from his injuries.Also read: Machchhar tells Netanyahu chilling flydubai cockpit ordealIsrael: The destinationThe flight was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv, carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, most of them Israeli nationals. After the cockpit attack sent the aircraft plunging, the plane was diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia. The passengers later continued their journey to Israel on a replacement flydubai aircraft.The incident has since raised questions about security checks for foreign airlines flying into Israel. Netanyahu ordered tighter checks on pilots flying to Israel, while Israeli investigators are expected to participate in the UAE-led probe. The issue has become particularly sensitive because Oman, the co-pilot’s home country, does not have diplomatic relations with Israel. Netanyahu has questioned how an Omani national came to be assigned to an Israel-bound flight.Also read: Did Israel ignore warnings? UAE shared info about flydubai crew & Omani co-pilotOman: The co-pilot and questions over his pastThe alleged attacker, identified as Hammam al-Hammami, is an Omani national. UAE authorities have described the incident as an attempted “terrorist attack”, saying he attacked the captain with a crash axe and tried to take control of the aircraft. The motive remains under investigation, and Oman has not publicly commented on the case.The biggest question around Oman is al-Hammami’s reported history. People familiar with the investigation told Reuters that he had previously been employed by Oman Air, while other reports said he had been barred from flying because of concerns over extremist views and was moved to an administrative role. He later left Oman Air. Reuters also reported that he underwent three months of training with Royal Air Maroc in 2025 but was not selected for employment. These details have intensified questions over how he subsequently came to work for flydubai and operate a flight to Israel.Saudi Arabia: Where the plane landedSaudi Arabia became part of the story because the aircraft was flying over Saudi territory when the cockpit attack sent it into a steep descent. After passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, reserve pilots aboard the flight took control and landed the aircraft at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities detained the co-pilot there.The country also became an early centre of the investigation. Netanyahu said Saudi authorities would interrogate the co-pilot, while Indian authorities in Saudi Arabia worked with local officials to assist Machchhar and his family. Thepilot was subsequently transferred from Saudi Arabia to Abu Dhabi after his medical condition improved.Also read: Crew of flydubai demanded release of co-pilot after he attacked Smit, claim flyersUAE: The flight, airline and the investigationThe UAE is central to the case because the flight originated in Dubai and is operated by flydubai, which is owned by the Dubai government. More importantly, the UAE is leading the investigation into what happened aboard Flight FZ1073. On October 3, UAE Prosecutor General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi officially described the incident as an attempted “terrorist attack”, saying the co-pilot used a cockpit crash axe to attack the captain and tried to take control of the aircraft.The UAE is also facing questions over how al-Hammami was cleared to work as a flydubai pilot given the reports about his reported employment history. Israeli officials have raised concerns about the security vetting of foreign crew, while the UAE-led investigation is examining the co-pilot’s motives and whether anyone else was involved. Israel is expected to participate in the probe.Australia: Intelligence file on co-pilot?Australia has entered the picture because co-pilot al-Hammami reportedly studied in Melbourne. Reuters reported that two sources briefed on the investigation said he attended a university there, while local reports identified the institution as RMIT University.Australia is now launching an investigation into the “links to Australia” of flydubai co-pilot Hammam al-Hammami. The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team, comprising the Australian Federal Police, Victoria Police and ASIO, confirmed that it was examining his links to Australia and if he was radicalised there, as per ABC Australia."The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team (VIC JCTT), comprising the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO, can confirm it is investigating the man's links to Australia. An update will be provided at an appropriate time," an Australian Federal Police (AFP) spokesperson said, referring to the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation.Two sources briefed on the investigation told Reuters that al-Hammami had studied at a university in Melbourne, with local media identifying it as RMIT University. The Financial Times separately also reported that al-Hammami had allegedly visited radical mosques and extremist websites while in Australia, and that Australian intelligence services had held a file on him.You use AI every day. articles.title: Family of teenager killed in crash to sue acquitted driver
articles.summary: Kyle Marshall and another teenager died when a car driven by Charles Gray span out of control in Stirling two years ago.
articles.body:
The family of a teenager killed in a car crash near Stirling two years ago are launching a civil case against the driver who was cleared of causing death by careless driving.

Kyle Marshall, 19, and Jayden McConnell, 17, died when a car driven by Charles Gray spun out of control and into the path of a lorry on the A91 near Bannockburn Interchange in March 2024.

Gray, who had passed his test a month earlier, was acquitted of causing the deaths of his two friends after a five-day trial at Stirling Sheriff Court last November.

According to the Scottish Sun, the Marshall family are now suing Gray for a six-figure sum, alleging negligence.

A spokesman for Digby Brown, the law firm representing the Marshall family, confirmed: "A civil action has now been raised in the Court of Session on behalf of the loved ones of Kyle to help them secure answers, support and recognition.

"It would be inappropriate to comment further at this time however we will continue to support the Marshall family during this time."

Teenage driver cleared of causing deaths of his best friends

The trial heard that Gray, who was 17 at the time of the crash, had lost control of the Vauxhall Corsa on a wet Sunday afternoon, on a stretch of road known as "greasy corner" because it had a reputation for becoming slippery.

Soon after leaving a roundabout, the car spun onto the opposite side of the carriageway and was hit by a heavy tipper lorry coming in the other direction.

Kyle Marshall and Jayden McConnell, in the rear of the vehicle, were killed while Gray's then girlfriend, Lauryn Moir, who was in the front passenger seat, survived without serious injury.

Gray himself was initially not breathing but an ambulance crew, who were passing the crash scene by chance, opened his airway, saving his life.

He was very badly injured with a ruptured spleen, spine damage and a brain injury.

Often choking back tears during his evidence, he said he could remember nothing of the crash itself and only learned what had happened to his friends when he woke up from an induced coma four weeks later.

The trial heard that analysis of an insurance company "black box" showed that Gray had been a "perfect driver" in the weeks before the collision.

The court was also told that police had not tested how slippery the road was or carried out a number of checks that might have established if there was a fault with the vehicle.

articles.title: Yemen’s Saudi-backed government announces major offensive against Iran-backed Houthis
articles.summary: ‌Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the beginning of a major military operation to turn back recent advances by the Houthi militant group.
articles.body: ‌Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the beginning of a major military operation to turn back recent advances by the Houthi militant group. Last month, the Iran-backed Houthis carried out a lightning offensive down the Red Sea coast, successfully seizing control of a key port and further putting pressure on the safety of international shipping. The head ​of Yemen’s presidential council, ⁠Rashad al-Alimi, said in a televised speech on Sunday that the ‌military ⁠operations aimed to reclaim the ​remaining ​territory held ‌by Houthis ⁠and restore ​state ​authority across the ⁠country. An offensive had been widely expected amid dozens of Saudi airstrikes against Houthi positions and further Houthi gains in southern Yemen. Al-Alimi said the decision to launch operations followed “the Houthi militias’ continued mobilization, escalation and attacks, as well as their threats against civilians, facilities, neighboring countries, and international shipping lanes.” The Houthis reported Saudi airstrikes against the capital Sanaa Saturday and again early Sunday. The Saudi coalition did not confirm the strikes. In retaliation for more than 50 airstrikes against Sanaa and other locations, the Houthis claimed Sunday that they had struck vital Saudi energy facilities. “The first targeted Aramco company in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco company in the Khurais area,” a Houthi military statement said, causing large fires at the targeted sites. There has been no word from the Saudis on the claimed strikes. The renewed fighting has already forced tens of thousands of people from their homes, and what happens next could shift the balance of power in Yemen and further disrupt shipping through the Red Sea. Early in September, the Houthis took a swath of Yemen’s Red Sea coast as far south as the critical Bab al Mandeb waterway, a chokepoint for commercial shipping crossing into the Indian Ocean. They announced that Saudi shipping trying to use the strait would be targeted, threatening additional pressure on global trade and energy routes. The Houthis have fired ballistic missiles and drones at multiple targets in Saudi Arabia since late July, including industrial and energy infrastructure. Much of the recent fighting has been in the southern region of Taiz, as the Houthis have sought to cut off government forces in the regional capital. The Houthis claimed on Sunday to have taken a critical highway linking Taiz with the seat of the Yemeni government in Aden. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: A Michigan collector paid $30 for a seashell painting at an estate sale; it was later identified as a 1951 Gertrude Abercrombie work; now it has sold in New York for a record $1,352,600!
articles.summary: Everyone peeks at an estate sale. He did too. He thought he would get his hands on some records or perhaps some mid-century furniture.
articles.body: Everyone peeks at an estate sale. He did too. He thought he would get his hands on some records or perhaps some mid-century furniture. That’s when he saw a painting hanging in the dark corner of a hallway. For most people, it may not necessarily have been an extraordinary painting. All there was on the 8-by-11-inch canvas were some seashells. Most buyers’ eyes would slide past such works, but this man’s didn’t. He spotted a signature on it that read: Abercrombie. He knew it was valuable. The painting was up for sale for $30. He didn’t think twice. He bought it.A few months later, five phone bidders and several online bidders competed for the painting at Freeman’s in New York. The auction house had estimated it would sell for $150,000 to $250,000. And on October 1, the hammer fell at $1,060,000! Along with the buyer’s premium, it came to $1,352,600. Imagine making a fortune out of $30! Well, this work was especially prized. No work by Gertrude Abercrombie had ever gone above $1 million. This one was quite rare! And only the right person saw its value.The Milwaukee exhibition that changed everythingThe buyer, who chose to stay anonymous, saw the signature on the painting while purchasing it at the estate sale in Kalamazoo, Michigan. But, as a longtime collector, he already knew it was not proof. He changed his family holiday plans to visit the Gertrude Abercrombie exhibition The Whole World Is a Mystery at the Milwaukee Art Museum. In the exhibition catalogue, he found a 1952 Chicago Tribune photograph of the painting in its original frame, displayed alongside the actual shells Abercrombie had painted. The photograph gave him an idea of what he had. Dr Susan Weininger, the leading Abercrombie scholar and a professor emerita of art history at Roosevelt University, also looked at it. She authenticated it. It was real. Things progressed soon. The buyer gave it to Freeman’s to sell, knowing the auction house had sponsored the Milwaukee exhibition.A rare painting from 1951Painted by Gertrude Abercrombie, a Chicago Surrealist artist, the painting Alderman Merriam’s Shells had been missing from public view for 75 years. The work depicts nine finely rendered seashells on a slate-grey surface, with a single conical shell suspended by a thread against a black wall, appearing to levitate above the rest. The shells were real, and so was their owner. Robert Merriam was alderman of Hyde Park, the Chicago neighbourhood where Abercrombie lived and worked. Hence the title.“A rare instance of the artist painting directly from life, it confirms that the shell motif in her later solitary shell paintings, long presumed invented, was drawn from observation and memory,” the auction house said in a release.The painting was exhibited in six solo shows in 1952 and 1953. Abercrombie gave it to Dr John Reynolds of Kalamazoo, Michigan, in exchange for medical services. The photograph stayed with his family until its rediscovery this year.“No fairytale would be complete without a storybook ending, and Gertrude Abercrombie’s Alderman Merriam’s Shells selling for a new auction record is as happily ever after as it gets. As happy as we are to have recaptured the record sale price for an artist we have long championed, we are even happier for our eagle-eyed consignor who saved this masterpiece from staying forever lost to time. I love it when good things happen to good people and when the story unfolds in reality just as we wrote it. The Abercrombie shooting the moon was obviously the high point of the day, but the rest of the sale shone bright, with great results across the board to add to the magic of the day,” said Zack Wirsum, Senior Vice President, Head of Department, Post War & Contemporary Art, speaking about the sale.And just like that, a painting found at an estate sale for $30 made over a million dollars.You use AI every day. articles.title: Brazilians head to polls in high-stakes, polarized election as Lula faces Flavio Bolsonaro
articles.summary: BRASILIA— Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday in the first round of a narrowly split election after a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of U.S. meddling.
articles.body: BRASILIA— Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday in the first round of a narrowly split election after a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of U.S. meddling. Leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, is seeking a fourth term, while Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, hopes to return his father’s right-wing ⁠movement to power. A victory for the senator would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with U.S. President Donald Trump, while Lula’s reelection could create a headache for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security. Despite growing worries over Brazil’s public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign has offered meager policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates. If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes, the top two will face off on October 25. Surveys show Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro polling roughly even in a likely runoff. Other candidates, including former state governors Ronaldo Caiado and Romeu ⁠Zema, have struggled to break through with the polarized electorate, even as Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro are ​each rejected by ⁠roughly half of voters, polls show. Flavio Bolsonaro has promised to seek amnesty for his father, who is serving a sentence of more than 27 years for plotting a coup after his narrow election defeat in 2022. Lula has cast the election as a choice between “democracy and denialism” and repeatedly warned of foreign interference. The Trump factor The fallout ⁠from Jair Bolsonaro’s conviction last year has colored much of the campaign. Trump, who called that case a “witch hunt,” imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, explicitly linking the ​tariffs to the trial ⁠of Bolsonaro after lobbying from the Bolsonaro family to pressure Brazil’s Supreme ‌Court to drop the charges. This year, Trump levied new tariffs over alleged unfair trade practices. Lula has cast the move as an attempt to sway the election and portrayed the Bolsonaros as too eager to please Washington at Brazil’s expense. Lula’s allies have warned that the Trump administration might refuse to recognize election results if he wins. They point to a failed effort to ‌send US officials to Brazil in order to “discuss electoral integrity,” according to the US State Department. Reuters reported on Wednesday that ‌Brazilian intelligence officials briefed a French and German delegation on alleged US and Russian interference before the election. The US has rejected claims of interference in Brazil’s affairs. Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he hosted Senator Flavio Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly. The senator, who has pledged closer ties with the U.S. and Israel, welcomed the Trump administration’s designation of Brazil’s major gangs as terrorist groups, which Lula rejected. Also in play is U.S. access to Brazil’s vast critical ⁠mineral reserves, key to Washington’s push to reduce dependence on China for those materials. Economic headwinds Despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity. Flavio Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns, while Lula has moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families. Rising spending and public debt above 82% of GDP have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil’s president may need to address. The government lowered its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to just 2.0% and 2.3% respectively. “Lula would likely preserve a state-led model with only modest spending restraint; Bolsonaro would likely pursue a more market-friendly agenda centered on spending cuts, privatizations, concessions, and a stronger fiscal anchor,” said Alberto Ramos, chief Latin America economist at Goldman Sachs. Scandal-plagued campaign Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed ‌much of Brazil’s political class and renewed public anger over corruption. Daniel Vorcaro, who ran the bank, was arrested earlier this year and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme. ​The investigation has probed the banker’s ties to figures from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to Flavio Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for money laundering tied to ‌the case by the federal police. The senator has denied any wrongdoing, although he confirmed raising ⁠millions of dollars from Vorcaro to make a movie about his father. The banker’s connections to Moraes, seen by many as a Lula ally, plunged the court into crisis ⁠a month before the vote, creating fresh problems for the president. Moraes has said the case is politically and electorally motivated for his conviction of the elder Bolsonaro. Lula has also tried to distance himself from a federal police investigation into his son ‌over alleged influence peddling, which his son denies. On Sunday, voters ​will also elect all 513 lower house members and two-thirds of the Senate, where some lawmakers ‌have pushed to impeach Moraes. Congress has gained greater influence in Brazilian politics since the impeachment ​of former President Dilma Rousseff, a Lula ally, in 2016, raising the stakes of those legislative races.

articles.title: Former BJD MLA attacked during padyatra in Jajpur
articles.summary: Former BJD MLA Pranab Balabantaray’s convoy attacked during Jan Sampark Padyatra in Jajpur; SUV vandalised. Police probe on; BJP-linked MLA denies role.
articles.body: Kendrapada: Tension erupted after armed miscreants attacked former BJD MLA Pranab Balabantaray and his convoy in the presence of police personnel at Madhupurgada village in Jenapur area of Jajpur district on Sunday. While Balabantaray escaped unhurt, his SUV was vandalised. The BJD supporters later staged a demonstration outside the office of the Jajpur superintendent of police (SP), demanding immediate arrest of those responsible.“We will arrest all the accused persons in this case. Security has been tightened in the area,“ said SP Yashpratap Shrimal.In his police complaint, Balabantaray accused Dharamasala’s BJP-backed independent MLA Himanshu Sekhar Sahoo and his supporters of attacking him during the BJD’s Jan Sampark Padayatra.“Criminal activities are on the rise in Jajpur district because of the BJP-backed MLA and his goons. Videos show the hooliganism in front of the police personnel,” Balabantaray said. He requested the police to preserve and examine CCTV camera footage, mobile phone videos, photographs and other evidence, besides recovering the weapons and identify all people involved.When contacted, MLA Sahoo denied the charges and said the BJP never gives shelter to any criminals. “Our supporters are not involved in the incident. Let the police probe and find out the truth.
